## 2026-08-13 · SAVE v15 — THE PRE-BILLING TAIL, THE PROBE SAGA, AND A RETRACTION (docs-only)

⚠️ **Numbering note:** the prompt for this save was labelled "v12", but v12/v13/v14 are already committed and
these passes came *after* v14. Recorded as **v15** — reusing a tag would have corrupted the record.

**Chapter ⑧ closes.** `DO-TOKEN-1` (`92c7b9b`) · `DO-STAR-1` (`5864514`) · `DO-SUP-1` (`9eebdb5`) ·
`DO-PROBE-1`/`DO-PROBE-2` (`600f1bc`, `5f96247`) · `DO-PLATE-1` (`568cdd3`) + `dd5ecb9`. **Canon: §N.20**, six
sub-sections.

⚠️ **THE HEADLINE IS A RETRACTION, NOT A FIX.** The "product-wide AA floor defect" reported at `8440b7e` was our
own instrument's **anti-alias halo** read from inside a dense 12px box. The true card floor is **4.50–4.67** and
`DesignTokenContrastTest`'s constant (4.55) sits inside it — **the constant is sound.** The tell was that the
box-interior median read *darker* than the true plate immediately beside the same text, which is impossible for
a real plate: only ink-blend darkens at the glyphs.

⚠️ **A finding is not safer for being ours.** A self-authored, already-committed conclusion deserves *more*
scrutiny, because sunk cost and face cost both push the other way. Both stale register entries are annotated
rather than deleted, and the 45 flags are marked **artefacts, not a work list**.

### The six syntheses folded into §N.20

1. **The instrument saga** — four corrections to one tool, every one a *plausible* number caught by a
   known-answer fixture. Durable: plausible beats crashing only in appearance · anchor-validation proves it sees
   *something*, not the *right plate* · **"validated" is per-input-class — name the untested classes** · sample
   the element's OWN box · worst pixel ≠ worst position under AA · commit the harness · fail loud with
   N/K/M counts · **"publish nothing" governs a clean bill too**.
2. **The retraction** (above).
3. **The headroom posture — ruled A (accept)**, with the ⛔ **floor-guard rider**: the test asserts a *constant*,
   so drift would not red it; re-point it at the true composited worst plate. Rides into the sweep.
4. **Verified-fine structurally** — the strongest §N.8d safeguard is a **missing field** (`DO-SUP-1`); and a
   comment documenting a deliberate *absence* is the good kind, because it stops a helpful "fix".
5. **Close a drift vector structurally** (`DO-TOKEN-1`) — a shell cannot diverge a token it no longer declares;
   **and the list your proof iterates over is itself an instrument** (the hand-typed set invented 7, omitted 13).
6. **An accessible name can be correct-then-overridden**, and **reveal-on-hover is tabbable-but-invisible**
   (`DO-STAR-1`) — both found *beside* a concern that was itself fine.

### State

The pre-billing tail is complete. Billing CODE + BUILD complete; the flip is gated only on the founder's Stripe
dashboard steps and the open VAT-validation decision. The contrast probe is **validated, with two named scope
gaps** (dense-small-text on a steep gradient; text over a photo). The AA floor is **sound**. The last design
pass — `DO-EMAIL-5-continued` (Part A 8 of 9, Part B 67) — is **unblocked** and carries the floor-guard rider.

## 2026-08-13 — SAVE v16 · THE A11Y FAMILY, AXIS 3 PROVEN, AND THE CHECKED CAPTURE CONTRACT

Capstone for the five passes after v15 (`921dae3`, `923435d`, `bcbc651`, `2b11af6`, `43e9f0d`).
Full canon: **§N.21** in `docs/PROJECT-STATE.md`. Decisions locked here:

1. **Posture A STANDS, and its premise is CORRECTED.** `--vy-faint` on the true measured worst plate is
   **4.4953**, not the 4.50 the decision was taken on — a 0.005 AA miss invisible at 2 decimals. Resolved
   **non-destructively**: the AA test keeps the derived plate (4.55) and the measured floor is pinned
   **separately as a fact**, so the drift vector is closed without darkening a token (option B, declined) or
   loosening the bar to 4.49. ⚠️ **The 0.005 is an OPEN FOUNDER CALL.**
2. ⚠️ **The 0.005 does NOT overturn the retraction.** §N.20.2 said the true floor is ~4.50 and SOUND (the
   4.19/4.07 was an instrument halo). The 0.005 **refines ~4.50 to 4.4953**. Both stand; see §N.21.2.
3. **A token that MISSES AA is a required fix; one that PASSES is not.** `--vy-on-grad` (4.33–4.48) and
   `--vy-accent-text` (3.82–4.46) were re-derived **by sampling** behind their real users;
   `--vy-on-grad-soft` **passed everywhere and was left unchanged**, and a guard asserts that non-change.
4. **Tokens are derived by SAMPLING, never by picking a stop** — the owner shell's O2/O7 rule now applies to
   the operator shell too (§N.8f cross-shell).
5. **A shared class is not fixed until every shell copy is** (`.vy-avatar`), and **a token with email/PDF
   mirrors moves everywhere at once** (`--vy-amber-text`; email 6.39 → 7.64, PDF 6.24 → 7.47).
6. **A broken capture must REFUSE, not fabricate.** The probe's contract (`viewportH`/`url`) is checked
   downstream and proven firing — the fifth and sixth corrections to this instrument.
7. **Axis 3 (DATA) is a first-class sweep axis**, alongside state (G10) and role (§N.14.1). Its throughput is
   iterative: **7 of 67 measured**; **"logged-unswept" means UNMEASURED, not fine.**

Canon: **§N.23**. Tooling only — no product code.

  painted colour is `alpha*text + (1-alpha)*plate`. The probe now MEASURES dimmed text instead of refusing it.
  Fixture hits the hand-computed 21.00 / **4.74** / **1.96** exactly, and ⚠️ **the model was validated against

## 2026-08-15 — DO13-4 · real password composition, at every set-password path

**One policy — `App\Support\Auth\PasswordPolicy`, registered as `Password::defaults()`:**
`min(8)->letters()->numbers()->symbols()`, plus the SENTENCE that describes it, in the same class so they
cannot drift apart.

⚠️ **THE AUDIT NAMED FOUR PATHS; THERE ARE NINE.** A sweep (validation arrays · the rule class however
aliased · `Hash::make` in app code) found five more the audit's list missed — **public self-signup**
(`OnboardingController`, the most public path in the product), the **platform-admin account**, and the
**entire guest realm** (Account · Claim · PasswordReset). ⚠️ The four were simply the ones an earlier reader
had already written down; §N.8f again — **a search finds only what you name**.

⚠️ **THE PROTOTYPES DO NOT AGREE, so "match the prototype" had no single answer** — "At least 8 characters"
(Set Password) · "at least 8 characters with a number." (Owner Security) · "8+ characters with a number and
symbol" (Guest Signup). A per-realm password policy would be a security smell and three more copies to
drift, so the **strongest promise became the floor for every realm**, and the weaker screens' copy was
corrected to state what is actually enforced. `letters()` is included ("characters with a number and symbol"
plainly means letters; without it `12345678!` passes); `mixedCase()` is NOT — no screen promises it, and
enforcing an unstated rule is the same defect reversed.

⚠️ **A NINTH SCREEN WAS FOUND ONLY BY SWEEPING THE ROUTE.** `livewire/operator/operator-security` has a
change-password form that stated NO rule at all — so a copy-sweep for "8 characters" could not see it,
precisely because it made no claim. Two screens were silent this way (the other: guest Account); both now
state the rule.

⚠️ **`CreatePlatformAdminCommand` deliberately NOT collapsed** — it requires min(12) + mixedCase + numbers +
symbols. Pointing it at the shared default would have WEAKENED it. Confirm-before-collapsing, the same
judgement the payout-status maps needed; a test pins the higher bar so a later tidy-up cannot lower it.

⚠️ **`uncompromised()` (Have-I-Been-Pwned) is an OPEN FOUNDER CALL, not a silent addition** (`DO13-4a`). It
is stronger, and it adds an outbound API dependency on every password set plus real UX friction — a product
decision. One line in `PasswordPolicy::rule()` if wanted; `hint()` must gain a matching sentence in the same
change, which is the whole point of the two living together.

**Composition is a SET-time rule, not a login rule** — existing users keep their passwords; a test proves a
legacy weak password still signs in. Seeders bypass validation (`Hash::make` directly) and are unaffected.
31 fixture passwords across 6 test files were strengthened — the FIXTURES, never the rule.

## 2026-08-15 — D24-2 · passkeys wired into the operator realm (reused, not rebuilt)

**Confirmed FIRST, because the audit has under-described before (DO13-4's four paths were nine) — this time
it was right:** `PasskeyService` contains **zero** owner references, `Passkey belongsTo(User)`, and
`PasskeyController` works on `$request->user()` throughout. Genuinely realm-agnostic, so the size stayed **S**
— a wiring pass, not a generalisation.

⚠️ **SIGN-IN NEEDED NO WIRING AT ALL**, which the audit suspected and this pass confirmed:
`PasskeyLoginController` runs on the shared `web` guard and resolves its destination through the shared
`RedirectsByRole` concern — the same one password login, 2FA and password reset use. An operator's passkey
already authenticated and already landed on `/app`. Only register + manage needed mounting.

- **The operator realm mounts the SAME controller** (`app.security.passkeys.*` alongside
  `owner.security.passkeys.*`) on the SAME service.
- ⚠️ **The owner's card was EXTRACTED into `<x-auth.passkeys>`, not copied.** Copying it would have been the
  faster wiring and the §N.8f defect this project keeps paying for — two markups, two ceremonies, drifting
  the first time either is touched. Only the route names differ, as props. A guard asserts neither page
  re-implements `navigator.credentials.create`.
- ⚠️ **A defect found while wiring (`D24-2a`):** the shared controller hardcoded `owner.passkey_registered` /
  `owner.passkey_removed`, so an **operator** registering a passkey would have written a **false realm into
  the audit trail** — the audit log's own §N.8d, invisible until someone read it back. Now realm-accurate by
  mount (`app.*` is the operator convention, per `app.trusted_device_revoked`). The flash key is resolved the
  same way — the two shells genuinely read different keys, a real difference rather than drift.

⚠️ **THE CEREMONY WAS PROVEN, NOT MERELY FLAGGED.** PHP cannot mint an authenticator signature, so the crypto
was exercised against the OPERATOR mount in Chromium with a CDP virtual authenticator: register via the real
button → credential persisted for the operator → the audit row read **`app.passkey_registered`** (which is how
that fix is known to WORK, not just to be present) → logged out → usernameless sign-in with a real signed
assertion → **landed on `/app/dashboard`**. So the realm-correct redirect is proven with real crypto rather
than inferred from the shared concern. Browser fixtures deleted, raw-query verified (0 passkeys, 0 audit rows).

⚠️ Reproducibility gotchas (both cost real debugging previously): WebAuthn **rejects an IP as `rp.id`** — use
`localhost:8000`, never `127.0.0.1:8000`; and usernameless sign-in needs a **discoverable/resident** credential.

**Untouched:** the WebAuthn service internals, the `Passkey` model, `PasskeyLoginController` (0-line diffs) and
every owner flow (re-verified — the owner page still renders its own routes and nothing else).

## 2026-08-15 — D3-4 · the last-year occupancy COVERAGE guard

**The defect, measured on the real data before a line changed:** operator occupancy divides room-nights-sold
by `SUM(availability.total)` — the rows that EXIST in the range — so Aug/Sep/Oct/Nov 2025 each rendered
exactly **50%**, computed over **2–3 days**, labelled as the month. The guard asked `roomNightsSold > 0`
(PRESENCE — "did anything sell?"), which three days of spine answers YES to. The question that matters is
"was this period actually MEASURED?"

- **`MetricSet` gained the coverage model** — `coveredDays` / `periodDays` / `coveragePct()` /
  `hasComparableCoverage()` — because that is where the denominator lives, so all consumers share ONE
  definition rather than each re-deriving it (§N.8f).
- ⚠️ **THE GUARD TESTS COVERAGE, NEVER THE VALUE, and that cuts both ways.** A thin month suppresses however
  HIGH its percentage; a fully-covered month publishes its real figure however LOW. Suppressing on the value
  would be the mirror-image defect — hiding true bad months, inventing an optimistic picture instead of a
  false one. Both directions are asserted, side by side, in one test.
- ⚠️ **THREE LY CONSUMERS, NOT THE ONE THE LEDGER NAMED.** It cited the occupancy-by-month guard. The **KPI
  deltas** (`isEmpty()` requires all three of sold/bookings/available to be zero, so a thin month is "not
  empty") and the **per-property pace row** were consuming the same figure — the latter would have kept
  badging a property "behind last year" against the number the page had just suppressed: the identical lie,
  one component over.

⚠️ **THE THRESHOLD IS A FOUNDER CALL, SURFACED WITH THE DATA (`D3-4a`).** Implemented: **SUPPRESS** at
**`MIN_COMPARABLE_COVERAGE_PCT = 80`**, a named constant, not a literal buried in a guard. The alternative —
CAVEAT ("based on N of M days") — was not chosen because a caveated number still gets anchored on.
⚠️ **The measured distribution is bimodal: prior-year months sit at 6–13% coverage, live months at 100%, with
NOTHING between 36% and 100%.** So the exact threshold is not delicate — any value in that gap separates the
two populations identically. One constant to change.

⚠️ **THE OWNER PATH IS UNAFFECTED AND UNTOUCHED** — `forOwnerUnits()` divides by `count(units) × days`, a
full-period denominator a thin spine cannot inflate. It now reports 100% coverage explicitly (stated rather
than inferred) and its figures render identically; browser-verified on `/owner/insights`.

⚠️ **Two silent failures caught by verifying rather than trusting.** `->distinct()->count('date')` compiled,
ran, and returned **0 for every period** — which would have suppressed EVERY comparison including the fully
covered ones, a worse and completely silent defect. And the first edit wired the coverage argument into the
OWNER call site while leaving the OPERATOR one on the 6-argument form — exactly backwards. Both were found by
probing real months, not by reading the diff.

⚠️ **A pre-existing test encoded the bug**: `OperatorAnalyticsTest`'s vs-last-year fixture recomputed only 10
of September's 30 days and asserted the comparison renders. The FIXTURE was made into the fully-measured month
it was always meant to represent; the rule was not relaxed.

Browser-verified: on the real demo data `/app/insights` now shows **no "Last year" series and no `pts` delta
pills** (the whole prior year is the 6–13% tail) while this-year figures render normally.

A real, GDPR-covered column that FRONT DESK already displayed and the dashboard's arrivals payload never
selected — so the same operator saw the guest's stated arrival at the desk and lost it on the dashboard.

carries values and the demo does not. That makes the **POPULATED** case the unrendered sibling branch, not

sources (payload idiom, Blade label, omit-when-null) and fails loudly on divergence. Extracting a shared
component — the `<x-auth.passkeys>` pattern from D24-2 — would remove the risk structurally.

⚠️ **A fixture trap worth recording:** the `book()` helper's overrides apply to the LINE only; the
reservation header's check_in/check_out are hardcoded to 2026-09-01, so a "today" override silently produced
a September booking that never appeared in today's arrivals and looked like the feature failing. Built
through the certified `AssignmentService` instead.

Browser-verified on the real demo: with a value forced, the dashboard and Front Desk print the identical
string `Arrival · late afternoon, after 6`; on a null arrival the dashboard row renders clean with no arrival
line at all. Fixture reverted, raw-query verified (0 of 41 populated).

## 2026-08-15 — D2-1 · `max_occupancy` on the reservation rack row

A real unit column the rack row payload never read, so an operator could not size a booking against the row
without leaving the screen.

⚠️ **THE LEDGER'S "POPULATED" HELD THIS TIME — 8 of 8 demo units carry 2–4.** D1-3's field was 0-of-41
because an action the demo never performs writes it; this one is set at unit creation. ⚠️ **That inverts
which branch hides: ZERO is the unrendered sibling here**, and it was forced both in the guard and in the
browser.

⚠️ **NULL IS IMPOSSIBLE; ZERO IS THE REAL EDGE.** `units.max_occupancy` is `int unsigned NOT NULL DEFAULT 2`
— the column can never BE null, but 0 is storable. And **0 does not mean "sleeps nobody", it means nobody
recorded a capacity.** "Sleeps 0" would assert a fact about a real unit that the data never claimed, so the
payload maps 0 → null and the view omits the element. Absent is the honest rendering of an unrecorded fact.

⚠️ **THE LABEL WAS MATCHED, NOT INVENTED (§N.8f).** The product already says **"Sleeps N"** in two places —
the operator Owner-detail unit list and the owner Unit-detail property row. The rack reuses that exact
wording and the row's existing muted meta class (`.vy-unit-name`) rather than introducing a third way to say
capacity on a dense row. A parity test reads those sources, so renaming the label in one place fails loudly.

⚠️ **IT IS THE UNIT'S CAPACITY, NEVER THE RESERVATION'S PARTY SIZE** — different fields on different tables,
and the two would look identical on a rack row. Proven by making them differ: a unit that sleeps 5 carrying a
stay for 2 renders "Sleeps 5".

**Logged, not built:**
- **`D2-1a`** — over-capacity detection is now cheap (capacity sits beside the bookings) but is LOGIC, not
  display, and needs a product decision: warn or block? at booking time or on the rack? what counts as a cot?
- **`D2-1b`** — ⚠️ the two EXISTING capacity surfaces render `Sleeps {{ … }}` **unguarded**, so both would
  print "Sleeps 0". Their comments reason correctly about NOT NULL but not about 0. Out of scope here; the
  rack is guarded.

Browser-verified on the real demo (§N.21.6): the rack rows read `101 · OUT OF SERVICE · Sleeps 2`, `A1 ·
Sleeps 4` …; with unit 102 forced to 0 its row renders as just `102` — no "Sleeps 0", no bare label, no broken
cell. Fixture reverted and raw-query verified back to the exact seeded values (8/8 populated, 2–4, zero zeros).

Two badges on one surface, both **reuse rather than rebuild**.

the dates. Both stay on the card — nothing about the existing `status` changed.

**Both are show-when-applicable**: no reservation → no stage chip (and never "Unknown"); not VIP → no badge,
which is almost every thread. A badge that appeared for everyone would say nothing.

`stage_meta` broke it. Fixed by stating the shape precisely rather than widening the declaration — the loose

because counting a needle in `__FILE__` counts the assertion itself. **A source-scanning guard has to exclude

## 2026-08-15 — D29-5 + DO6-4 · per-notification dismiss, both realms

Mark-read existed; a user could not take a notification OFF their feed. One shared mechanism now does:
`notifications.dismissed_at`, written by `NotificationController::dismiss` — the SAME shared controller
mark-read already used, mounted once in the shared `auth` group and reached by both realms.

⚠️ **THE LOAD-BEARING RISK WAS CONFLATION, NOT THE FEATURE.** Two tables now carry a `dismissed_at`:
`notifications` (this feature — take a row off MY feed) and `owner_attention_states` (a DIFFERENT entity —
the owner's "needs attention" SIGNAL, keyed by owner_id + attention_key, written by
`/owner/attention/dismiss`). Same column name, same word in the UI, unrelated meanings. Dismissing a
notification must never silence an attention signal — that would quietly remove a real to-do from an owner's
dashboard because they tidied their inbox. Asserted explicitly, mutation-proven (making dismiss write the
attention store REDS), and confirmed on the live demo: after a real browser dismiss, `notifications` had 1
dismissed row and `owner_attention_states` had 0.

⚠️ **DISMISS IS NOT MARK-READ.** Read = "I have seen this", the row STAYS; dismiss = "take this off my list",
the row LEAVES. Separate columns that coexist — a row can be read-and-dismissed or dismissed-while-unread.
Overloading `read_at` would have made the two acts indistinguishable and silently hidden everything a user
merely glanced at; a test asserts a dismissed row is dismissed WITHOUT being marked read.

⚠️ **ONE FILTER, IN THE ONE SHARED BUILDER.** `NotificationFeed` was already the single builder behind the
operator page, the owner page and the top-bar bell panel, so the `whereNull('dismissed_at')` lives there once
and every surface inherits it — including the unread COUNT, or a dismissed-but-unread row would keep the bell
lit pointing at something the user had explicitly cleared. A dismiss that hid a row on one surface but not
another would be worse than no dismiss at all.

**Self-only by construction**, exactly like the mark-read it parallels: the write goes through
`$request->user()->notifications()`, so another user's id does not resolve (404). Verified by RAW QUERY, not
through the same scoping that enforces it — and the converse is tested too, so the scope is not merely
"deny everything".

⚠️ **The dismiss control sits OUTSIDE the `@unless ($item['read'])`** that wraps mark-read in both feeds:
mark-read only makes sense while a row is unread, but an already-read notification can still be taken off the
list. Same form and button idiom as the tick beside it — no new control style.

⚠️ **Two of my own guard errors, both the self-reference shape:** a source check banning the word "attention"
failed on the controller's own anti-conflation docblock (tokenised, so it scans what RUNS, not what is
written about it), and a fixture wrote `notifiable_type` as the FQCN when the project enforces a morph map
(`'user' => User::class`) — the row inserted cleanly and was then invisible to `$user->notifications()`,
which looks exactly like the feature failing. Confirmed against the real demo rows rather than guessed.

`/attention/dismiss` and mark-read are byte-identical to before; DO6-2 (grouping) and D30-3 (digest) remain
separate.

## 2026-08-15 — D3-1 · a custom date range on operator Insights

⚠️ **THE ITEM WAS SMALL BECAUSE THE PLUMBING WAS ALREADY RIGHT — confirmed before building, not assumed:**
`resolveRange()` is ONE seam returning `['key','label','start','end']`, and everything below it consumes only
the two dates; the last-year comparison was ALREADY a span shift (`->subYear()` on both ends), so it is
correct for an arbitrary window with no change at all. The whole feature is a branch in that one method plus
a picker.

⚠️ **AND THE CONVERGENCE IS WHAT MAKES IT CORRECT, NOT MERELY TIDY.** D3-4's coverage guard lives on the
`MetricSet` that `forProperties()` returns. A custom range with its own metric path would have rendered the
exact fake-full-month prior-year figure D3-4 had just removed — **a regression introduced by a new feature
rather than by editing the fixed code.** The inheritance is asserted both ways: a custom window over a thin
prior year suppresses, and one over a fully-covered prior year still compares.

⚠️ **THE MAX SPAN IS DICTATED BY THE COMPUTATION, NOT BY TASTE.** `PerformanceMetrics::monthlyTrend*()` walks
months under a `$guard < 13`. Every PRESET is inside that cap, so it has never bitten — an arbitrary range is
the first thing that could reach it, and a 14-month window would have returned 13 bars under a heading
claiming more (§N.8d). The bound is enforced at the seam rather than by loosening a guard in the metric layer
this item must not touch, and a test reads the guard so the two are re-reconciled deliberately if it changes.

**Three smaller decisions worth recording:**
- **End-EXCLUSIVE.** `?to=` is the last day the user means to include; the metric windows are half-open, and
  every preset already adds a day. A custom window that stopped ON the typed date would have been the one
  range in the product that silently drops a day.
- **Backwards is REJECTED, not swapped.** Swapping would answer a different question while the fields still
  read the other way round. An unusable window falls back to a preset AND says so, keeping the typed values
  so they can be corrected — silence would show preset figures under fields claiming otherwise.
- **A plain GET form**, like the preset links: the range rides the URL, so it is shareable and bookmarkable
  and works without JavaScript.

⚠️ **Logged, not done (`D3-1a`):** the OWNER Insights has its OWN `resolveRange()` (3 presets to the
operator's 5) and no custom window. `CustomRange` is realm-agnostic so wiring it there is the same one
branch — but the two preset SETS already differ, and a range-picker item should not silently unify an
existing divergence.

⚠️ **A guard-authoring trap hit for the THIRD time this session:** the "no metric call in the resolver" check
grepped for `PerformanceMetrics::`, which the resolver's docblock legitimately NAMES to explain what it
deliberately does not call. Tokenised — a source-scanning guard must read what RUNS, not what is written
about it.

Browser-verified (§N.21.6): a custom Jul–Aug 2026 window renders labelled `1 Jul 2026 – 31 Aug 2026` with
**9 month-bars against the preset's 19** — the chart genuinely narrowed; a backwards window and a 14-month
window each show the rejection notice with their values kept. No fixture was needed (the range rides the
URL); the demo is unchanged.

## 2026-08-15 — MEMORY CHECKPOINT (SAVE v17) · the audit-and-feature-waves programme, captured

⚠️ **DOCS-ONLY — no code, no tests, no behaviour change.** This entry is the capstone over fourteen commits
that already each have their own dated entry above; it records what the CHAPTER means, not what each pass did.

**What the chapter is.** `a743bcd` → `b28122d`: a read-only audit of the whole backend, the three
"wrong-not-absent" corrections it found, then two waves of features run off its ledger. The canon is the new
**§N.27** in `PROJECT-STATE.md`; the RESUME block is rewritten to **SAVE v17** with the full shipped ledger.

⚠️ **THE AUDIT'S VERDICT IS THE FRAME, AND IT IS THE MOST USEFUL THING IN THE CHAPTER: THERE IS NO ROT.** Every
route resolves; there are zero stubbed actions and zero dead controls; exactly **three** items were *wrong*
rather than *absent*, and all three are fixed. That single finding reclassifies everything that follows —
the remaining feature work is **additive**, not repair, and it changes what "nearly done" means.

⚠️ **AND ITS COROLLARY IS THE PLANNING FACT: NOTHING ON THE FEATURE BACKLOG BLOCKS LAUNCH.** The gates are the
**deployment sprint** (zero deploy artifacts — and inside it the one crontab line the GDPR deletion and ID
purge silently depend on) and the **founder's Stripe/VAT steps**. Feature-completeness and launch-readiness are
different axes; shipping features does not move launch closer (§N.27.12).

**Two reconciliations, recorded because the method is the point:**

⚠️ **(1) THE BRIEF SAID `D3-1` WAS "IN FLIGHT — prompt written, NOT run". `git log` SHOWS IT SHIPPED AT
`b28122d`.** The source won: the ledger row is written from the commit. A checkpoint that transcribes a brief
over the history would bake a false "pending" into the one file a cold session trusts most.

⚠️ **(2) THE v16 RESUME'S OWN POINTER WAS STALE.** It told a fresh session to read "§N.13–§N.21" while
**§N.22–§N.26 already existed** (the restore/a11y tail), and its chapter list stopped at nine while eleven had
closed. **A handoff surface decays silently** — nothing fails when it goes stale, which is exactly why it has
to be re-read against the history rather than appended to. Both the pointer and the chapter count are corrected,
and chapter ⑩ now has a ledger row like every other.

**The decisions carried forward unchanged** (verified present, not rewritten): the billing rulings (pricing is
configurable DATA · per-unit prorates · €49/€99 **VAT-inclusive** · Stripe Tax Option B · plan CRUD) · the
restore rulings (`#E8703A` sub-AA **accepted**; the avatar/plan-tag plates flattened) · ⚠️ **`D3-4a` —
SUPPRESS at 80% coverage STANDS**, not caveat, because a caveated number still gets anchored on.

**Next is `DO3-3`** (failed-payout retry — money-adjacent: ⚠️ confirm what "retry" does and prove idempotency
against the certified rail's existing unique key + row-lock; a retry must not double-pay), then Waves 3–4.

⚠️ **The suite was NOT run for this checkpoint** — it is docs-only and touches no executable path. The last
measured baseline stands: **2185/2194, 14,065 assertions, 6 non-green** (the documented set).

## 2026-08-15 — DO3-3 · the failed-payout alert + retry ⚠️ MONEY-ADJACENT

**The ask:** a failed payout showed a status and no way to act. **The crux was what "retry" DOES**, and
confirming it changed the shape of the whole pass — in both directions (§N.27.11).

⚠️ **CONFIRMATION 1 — THE SERVICE ALREADY EXISTED, AND IT COULD DOUBLE-PAY.** `OwnerPayoutService::retry()`
was already written (append-only: a NEW `pending` payout superseding the failed one) and had exactly one
caller — a service test. It had **no idempotency of any kind**: no row lock, no re-check, no uniqueness. Two
calls wrote **two live payouts for one statement**, and `PayoutRunService::processOwner()` disburses *every*
pending payout an owner has, so both would have been sent. ⚠️ **The double-pay was dormant, not absent — and
adding any control would have shipped it.** The audit ledger described this item as "the status exists; the
affordance does not", which is a true sentence about the wrong half of the problem.

⚠️ **CONFIRMATION 2 — RETRY DOES NOT SEND, AND THAT IS WHAT MAKES IT SAFE FOR AN OWNER.** `retry()` re-QUEUES;
only `pay()` disburses, and `pay()` is operator-permissioned (`payouts.manage`) over the config-selected rail
(`manual` by default; `stripe_connect` is config-gated and test-mode). **So the owner gets no rail.**

⚠️ **CONFIRMATION 3 — SEAM, NOT LIVE.** Nothing in this pass touches live Stripe. Everything is proven against
the manual rail and a deliberately-failing test rail; `StripeSafetyGuard` and the founder's go-live steps are
untouched. `failed` is unreachable on the default rail at all (the manual rail cannot refuse), which is why
the failed state is an **unrendered branch** that had to be FORCED to verify.

**THE RECONCILIATION THAT MATTERS — a ratified refusal, re-read rather than overturned.** The design register
(§O3) refused the "Retry payout" button on the stated premise that **"there is no owner-initiated retry
RAIL"**. That premise is correct and is **still honoured**: this gives the owner a re-queue, never a rail. The
register's *other* refusal — the **"est. {time}" retry ETA** — has no source and **STANDS, unbuilt** (#39).
The banner half the register called a REAL GAP is what was built.

**Built:** `Payout::LIVE_STATUSES` (the ONE definition of "still claims this statement's money", now read by
BOTH writers — §N.8f) · a hardened `retry()` (transaction + `lockForUpdate` + in-lock status re-check + the
same one-live-payout-per-statement invariant `createFromStatement()` enforces) · the shared
`App\Support\Owner\PayoutRecovery` (ONE definition of retryable/blocked, read by the view gate AND the write
gate so the button and the guard cannot drift) · `owner.payouts.retry` (controller route #20, `$capPayout`
co-owner-only #28/#42, owner-scoped by `whereIn` over the per-capability owner set, throttled, audited) · the
failure alert on `/owner/payouts`.

⚠️ **RETRYABILITY IS DERIVED FROM REAL CURRENT STATE, NEVER THE STORED FAILURE STRING.** `failure_reason`
describes an attempt that is over; what decides the NEXT attempt is how the account stands now. So a blocked
account gets **fix-then-retry guidance** routed at the real page instead of a doomed re-send, and a cause the
owner has since fixed clears itself. The blockers mirror the Connect rail's OWN refusals and a drift test pins
them to it.

⚠️ **A LIVE §N.8d FOUND BESIDE THE FLAGGED ITEM (§N.13.1, holding again).** The lifecycle note told owners
*"The last payout failed; it will be retried as a new payout."* **Nothing retried anything** — no scheduler, no
job, and no control. Corrected to what is true, and guarded.

**Proven:** 14 tests; **6 mutations, each verified to have landed.** ⚠️ **M1 exposed a hole in the TESTS, not
the code:** removing the service's live-payout guard reded only ONE of the three double-pay tests — the other
two were passing on the *controller's* pre-flight, so the service guard could have been deleted silently while
every non-HTTP caller double-paid. **Per-layer tests were added (§N.4p) and M1 then reded all three.** Also:
`grep -c` with a shell-mangled pattern reported a restore had failed when it had not — **verify a revert with
a fixed-string match** (§N.27.6, one more way a check lies).

Browser-verified as the demo owner on a FORCED failure (§N.21.6): the alert renders the real €885.60 /
September 2026 / the rail's own reason / the real attempt date and **no ETA**; Retry queues exactly one payout;
the control then **disappears**, replaced by the honest "already on its way"; a second POST creates nothing
(2 rows, 1 audit event). ⚠️ **Fixture fully reverted — the `payouts` table diffs byte-identical to its
pre-pass snapshot** (6 rows, `updated_at` included), zero orphan rows, zero residual audit/domain events; the
demo Sep net **€885.60 unchanged**.

**Untouched:** the payout computation · the tax-hold engine · the status vocabulary and badges
(`processing`→"In transit" / `held`→"On hold", DO-CORRECTNESS-1) · live Stripe. Suite **2208 / 2199**,
14,163 assertions, 6 non-green = the documented set; PHPStan L5 (0); Pint clean.

⚠️ **LOGGED, NOT BUILT:** the OPERATOR has no retry control either — `pay()`'s permission holder still cannot
re-queue a failed payout from `/app/payouts/run`. The hardened service is ready for it; wiring it is a
separate item and a separate surface.

## 2026-08-15 — DO9-2 · save an Add-Unit request as a DRAFT (+ resume)

**The ask:** the Add-Unit wizard was submit-or-lose. **The confirm step found that the missing state was the
easy half — the dangerous half was what would happen the moment it existed.**

⚠️ **THE LOAD-BEARING FINDING — THE OPERATOR QUERY HAD NO STATUS FILTER AT ALL.**
`OperatorUnitRequests` read `UnitRequest::query()->…->get()`, every row, unfiltered. Adding a `draft` state
without touching it would have put **every half-finished wizard on the operator's desk immediately** — an
owner's private, deliberately-unsent work shown to staff, and shipped inside a feature whose entire promise is
"nothing is sent until you submit." The exclusion now lives in ONE place, `UnitRequest::scopeFiled()`, which
the review list AND its KPI counts both read (§N.8f), rather than in a filter each future operator surface
would have to remember.

⚠️ **TWO MORE PREMISES THE LIVE SCHEMA AND THE LIVE CODE CORRECTED** (read them, don't assume — §N.27.2):

- **`requested_name` was `NOT NULL` with no default.** A draft of a wizard the owner has barely opened is
  exactly the case with no name, so the feature was physically unstorable until the column became nullable.
  ⚠️ It is nullable ONLY for drafts: `required` still stands in the SUBMIT rules, so every FILED request has a
  name. The owner's list labels a nameless draft "Untitled draft" rather than rendering a blank row.
- **`requestStatusMeta()`'s `default` arm reads "Pending review".** A draft would have been labelled as
  already-with-the-operator — the precise opposite of the truth, on the one screen where that distinction IS
  the feature. A too-loose default, §N.27.5's shape again. Named explicitly and guarded.

**Built:** `draft` added to the real `status` enum by ALTER (**the state machine EXTENDED — never a parallel
draft table**), lifecycle now **draft → pending → approved | declined** · `saveDraft()`/`findDraft()` beside
`submit()`, all three over ONE private `persist()` so a draft and a submission cannot drift into storing
different things · ONE `rules()` behind both writes · `owner.add-unit.draft` (controller route #20,
`$capActions` co-owner-only, the same gate as submit) · resume as a plain `?draft={id}` GET that pre-fills the
wizard · Save-as-draft on every step, in the wizard's own ghost-button idiom.

⚠️ **THE RELAXATION IS REQUIREDNESS, AND NOTHING ELSE.** A draft may be INCOMPLETE but never MALFORMED: the
kind whitelist, the numeric bounds, the amenity-existence check, the 2,000-char note cap and the photo
mime/size limits are byte-identical in both contexts. A draft that saves cleanly cannot fail submit-time
validation for a reason the owner was never shown — and **submit re-validates in full**, so an incomplete
draft is rejected at submit (mutation-proven).

⚠️ **`findDraft()` PINS `status = 'draft'`, AND THAT IS A GUARD, NOT A TIDINESS.** Without it a resumed-draft
submit could be aimed at an ALREADY-FILED request id and would rewrite, from the owner's side, a request the
operator had already seen or approved. Proven: passing a filed id files a NEW request and leaves the original
byte-identical.

**Placement detail worth keeping:** Save-as-draft sits **after** "Submit for review" in DOM order on purpose.
Implicit submission (Enter) targets the FIRST submit button in a form, so placing it earlier would have made
Enter on step 4 silently save a draft instead of submitting — quietly breaking the Enter guard the form's own
comment describes.

**Proven:** 13 tests; **4 mutations, each verified to have landed** — re-including drafts in the operator query
reds the leak test AND the source guard; removing the draft relaxation reds the partial-save; relaxing SUBMIT
reds the incomplete-submit; dropping the scope+status pin on `findDraft()` reds both the cross-owner and the
rewrite-a-filed-request tests. ⚠️ The isolation is asserted against the **operator's own Livewire component**
and the scope directly, per DO3-3's M1 lesson — never through an owner-side path another filter protects.

Browser-driven end to end as the demo owner: a name-only wizard saved → redirected to `?draft=…` pre-filled →
**the operator's Unit-requests screen showed "No unit requests yet · 0 pending"** → resumed via Continue
("Draft — not sent", not "Pending review") → completed → submitted → the SAME row promoted to `pending`, one
row total. ⚠️ **§O9's Alpine-root trap was walked into a third time** (`document.querySelector('[x-data]')`
matches the SHELL's root, not the wizard's) — the component root has to be selected by its own state.

⚠️ Fixture fully reverted — `unit_requests` diffs **identical** to its pre-pass snapshot, no orphan media,
amenity-pivot or audit rows.

**Untouched:** the submit flow's full validation · the operator review beyond the draft exclusion · DO9-1's
notes (which round-trip through the draft) · isolation/RBAC. **DO9-3 (withdraw) deliberately not built.**
Suite **2221 / 2212**, 14,239 assertions, 6 non-green = the documented set; PHPStan L5 (0); Pint clean.

## 2026-08-15 — DO9-3 · withdraw a submitted unit request

**The lifecycle is now complete: draft → pending → approved | declined | withdrawn.** `withdrawn` is a fifth
value on the same enum DO9-2 extended (§N.8f) — a **soft transition, never a delete**, so the record still
shows what the owner asked for, when, and that they took it back. Deleting would erase a request the operator
may already have read and make "what happened to that villa request?" unanswerable.

⚠️ **THE RACE IS THE FEATURE, AND IT IS DECIDED UNDER A LOCK.** The owner's page is a SNAPSHOT: by the time
they click Withdraw, the operator may already have approved the request and created a real, bookable unit
from it. `withdraw()` therefore re-reads the row with `lockForUpdate()` and re-checks `pending` **inside** the
lock; a request that has moved on is refused, and the refusal names the state that actually won ("your manager
already approved this request"). Retracting there would have told an owner their request was cancelled while
live inventory existed for it.

⚠️ **THE MUTATION THAT DID NOT RED — AND WHAT IT EXPOSED.** Replacing `$locked->status` with the caller's
`$request->status` (i.e. defeating the in-lock re-check entirely) left **all ten tests green**. The reason is
worth keeping: over HTTP the controller re-loads the request fresh, so the caller's copy is never stale and a
gate reading it passes too — **the tests proved the state GATE but not that it reads the LOCKED row.** The
real race needs a genuinely stale in-memory model: load while pending, let the operator approve, then act. A
test that forces exactly that was added, and the mutation then reds. **DO3-3's M1 lesson, recurring: a guard
is only proven by a mutation that can actually reach it.**

⚠️ **LOGGED, NOT FIXED — THE REVERSE RACE IS STILL OPEN.** `approve()` and `decline()` check `pending`
**outside** their transaction and take no row lock, so an approve already in flight can land on top of a
completed withdrawal and create a unit for a retracted request. Withdraw cannot defend against that from its
own side; guarding those two certified operator paths is a separate change and was deliberately not made here.
**This pass closes owner→operator, not operator→owner.**

⚠️ **THE LABEL TRAP, ONE STATE LATER.** `requestStatusMeta()`'s `default` arm reads "Pending review" — the
same helper that would have mislabelled a draft in DO9-2 would have told an owner their just-retracted request
was still live with the operator. Named explicitly and guarded. The OPERATOR side had the same shape in a
different medium: its tone ternary falls through to the AMBER "needs attention" colour, so a withdrawn request
would have carried the label *Withdrawn* while the colour still said *pending*. `withdrawn` joins `declined`
on the muted tone.

**Visibility ruling:** `withdrawn` **is** a filed status, unlike `draft`. A draft was never sent; a withdrawn
request genuinely was, and the operator may have been mid-review — so it stays visible and labelled while
being non-actionable (every operator action is gated on `pending`) and absent from the pending count.

**Built:** the enum ALTER · `OwnerUnitRequestService::withdraw()` (transaction + `lockForUpdate` + in-lock
re-check + a real, state-specific refusal) · `owner.add-unit.withdraw` (controller route #20, `$capActions`,
owner-scoped resolve → cross-owner 404) · a Withdraw control on pending rows only, with the realm's existing
`onsubmit confirm` idiom · audited (`owner.unit_request_withdrawn`, before/after recorded).

**Proven:** 11 tests; **4 mutations, each verified to land** — removing the gate reds three tests; defeating
the in-lock re-check reds the stale-copy test (added because of it); dropping the "Withdrawn" label arm reds
the label test; breaking the owner scope reds the cross-owner test. The gate is asserted at the **service** as
well as over HTTP, so a non-HTTP caller is gated too.

⚠️ **TWO ASSERTION TRAPS, BOTH DOCUMENTED, BOTH WALKED INTO:** the wizard's live-preview card always carries a
"Pending review" badge, so a page-wide `assertDontSee('Pending review')` can never pass — the needle had to be
the status CHIP's own markup. And **`assertDontSee('Withdraw')` failed on a CSS COMMENT I had just written in
the shared layout** — CSS comments ship (§N.15.3); an absence assertion must read what RENDERS. Also: a fixture
that filed a request left the `unit_request_done` flash set, so the next render showed the **done confirmation
screen** rather than the requests list — the helper now burns that flash (§N.27.6).

Browser-driven as both realms: two pending requests, one withdrawn and one **approved behind the rendered
page** — the first retracted, the second **refused with the real reason**, one audit row. The operator screen
then showed **0 pending**, "Withdrawn" in muted grey, no actions. ⚠️ Fixture reverted — `unit_requests` diffs
identical to its pre-pass snapshot; zero withdrawn rows, zero audit residue.

**Untouched:** `approve()`/`decline()` (their gate mirrored, not modified) · DO9-2's draft + resume + the
operator draft-exclusion · the submit flow. **Also logged, not built:** there is no "discard draft" — a draft
is resumed or simply left, and deleting one is a different decision from retracting a filed request.
Suite **2232 / 2223**, 14,338 assertions, 6 non-green = the documented set; PHPStan L5 (0); Pint clean.

## 2026-08-15 — DO9-3b · the REVERSE race: approve()/decline() locked

**DO9-3 closed owner→operator and logged the other direction as open. This closes it.**

⚠️ **THE DEFECT, CONFIRMED BY READING AND THEN BY A RED TEST.** `approve()` checked `pending` on the CALLER'S
COPY, outside its transaction; `decline()` did the same and had **no transaction at all**. So an operator
approve already in flight could land on a request the owner had just withdrawn — and **create a real,
bookable unit for a retracted request**: inventory the operator is billed for, assigned to an owner who had
said no. That material side-effect is what made this worse than a stale status.

⚠️ **THE TESTS WERE WRITTEN FIRST, AND RUN AGAINST THE UNHARDENED CODE.** Five failed — including an approve
of a genuinely `withdrawn` request succeeding. Proving the defect *with the instrument that will later prove
the fix* is worth more than fixing first and asserting after: it shows the test can actually detect it.

**CONVERGED (§N.8f).** All three transitions now run through ONE private `transitionFromPending()`:
a transaction, a `lockForUpdate` on the request, and a re-check of **the LOCKED row's** status inside that
lock; `$apply` runs only on a row confirmed `pending` at that instant, and runs INSIDE the transaction.
`withdraw()` folded in behaviour-identically. One race-safety mechanism, not three copies that drift.

⚠️ **ATOMICITY IS THE POINT, NOT JUST THE GATE.** Approve's unit creation, the availability recompute, the
status write, the audit and the notification all sit inside the locked transaction, after the re-check — so
"refused" and "no unit" are the same fact rather than two things that have to agree. Mutation M3 (run the
side-effect *before* the gate) reds 6 tests.

⚠️ **THE REFUSAL MESSAGE STAYED WITH THE CALLER.** The mechanism is shared; the wording is not. The operator
paths speak to staff ("Only a pending request can be approved."); `withdraw()` speaks to the owner and names
which state beat them. Collapsing both into one sentence would have been de-duplication flattening a real
distinction (§N.16.5, §N.27.4) — the payout-map lesson, applied before it could bite.

**Also corrected inside the fix:** approve now builds the unit from the **locked** row (`requested_name`,
`sleeps`, `owner_id`, `currency`) rather than the caller's copy, and resolves the property/room type AFTER the
re-check — which keeps the failure ORDER unchanged (a non-pending request still refuses for being
non-pending, not for a bad property id) and resolves nothing for a request about to be refused.

**Proven:** 8 tests; **3 mutations, each verified to land.** ⚠️ **M1 is the one that matters**: replacing
`$locked->status` with `$request->status` — the exact mutation that passed DO9-3's entire suite — now reds
**five** tests, because every race test here forces a GENUINELY STALE in-memory model instead of going
through HTTP (where the controller re-loads fresh and the two are indistinguishable). M2 (remove the
re-check) reds six; M3 (side-effect before the gate) reds six.

⚠️ **A GUARD THAT READ ITS OWN DOCBLOCK, for the fourth time in this programme (§N.27.5).** The
"one lockForUpdate" assertion counted **three** — the code's one plus two mentions in the comments explaining
it. Tokenised with `token_get_all`, skipping `T_COMMENT`/`T_DOC_COMMENT`. A source guard must read what RUNS.

Browser-verified as the real operator: a pending request on screen → the owner withdrew behind the rendered
page → Approve → **"Only a pending request can be approved."**, the row flipped to Withdrawn, and **8 units
before, 8 after** with `created_unit_id` null and zero approve-audit rows. Fixture reverted; units and
requests identical to the pre-pass snapshot.

⚠️ **HONEST BOUND ON WHAT IS PROVEN.** These tests prove the **in-lock re-read** — that the decision uses the
database's current truth, not the caller's snapshot. They do not prove the **lock's** mutual exclusion under
genuine concurrency; that needs separate connections, which this repo already has a pattern for
(`tests/Support/*_race_worker.php`, as used for double-booking). Adding a worker-based test for these
transitions is **logged, not built**.

**Untouched:** what approve/decline DO in the normal case (unit created, statuses/notes/reviewer stamped,
owner notified — asserted unchanged) · withdraw's behaviour · isolation/RBAC/permissions. Suite **2240 /
2231**, 14,381 assertions, 6 non-green = the documented set; PHPStan L5 (0); Pint clean.

## 2026-08-15 — D1-1 · ticking a dashboard task (a personal note, not a completion)

⚠️ **THE FORK WAS NEITHER SHAPE THE BRIEF ANTICIPATED, AND READING THE CODE IS THE ONLY REASON WE KNOW.**
The brief framed this as either (A) a plain checklist `completed_at` or (B) a housekeeping completion that
marks a unit ready. It is neither. `OperatorDashboard::tasks()` **derives every row live** from real counts —
urgent work orders, rooms to clean, arrivals still to check in — and each row only exists while its count is
greater than zero. There is no task record to complete, no id, and no downstream state to move.

**So what would "done" have meant?** A flag asserting work is finished, sitting next to a number the product
can independently see is NOT zero. That is a fabricated status (#39), and the design register had already
warned about exactly it: *"a task whose real count is still >0 cannot be 'done'."*

**THE RESOLUTION — a PERSONAL, PER-DAY tick**, and the register's other open question ("a personal note or a
shared team signal — they are different tables") is answered **personal**, for two reasons: the prototype's
own persistence was `localStorage` (per-browser, per-person, non-authoritative), so personal is the faithful
translation rather than a compromise; and one person's tick must never hide urgent work from a teammate.

⚠️ **THE HONESTY INVARIANT, NOW A GUARD:** a ticked row is dimmed and struck **but keeps its real count and
stays on the list**, and the header distinguishes two genuinely different states — an EMPTY list means the
counts reached zero ("All caught up", true), while a fully-ticked list says *"you've ticked off all N — the
work itself is still open below"*. Ticking never changes a count, never removes a row, and never touches the
KPI card. A test resolves the real work and proves the row disappears **regardless of the tick**.

⚠️ **A SCHEMA TRAP AVOIDED BY REMEMBERING OUR OWN HISTORY.** The dashboard reads either one property or ALL
of them, so the natural column was a nullable `property_id` ("null = all"). In MySQL a UNIQUE index treats
NULLs as **distinct**, so the constraint would have been silently inert for every all-properties tick — the
exact defect `DO-CORRECTNESS-1` found on `guest_waitlist_entries`. `scope_key` is generated and NOT NULL, the
same fix, applied before it could bite.

**Built:** `operator_task_states` (unique on user + scope + task + date → **idempotent by construction, at the
database**) · a closed `OperatorTaskState::KEYS` set · stable string keys on each derived row (never an index —
the list changes shape as counts clear) · a self-only POST controller route (#20) taking the user from
`$request->user()` and the scope from `PropertyContext`, never the request · the tick control + an honest
progress line.

⚠️ **DELIBERATELY NO LOCK AND NO TRANSACTION.** This changes no count and moves no state, so DO9-3b's
machinery would be cargo here. The care went where the risk actually is: idempotency, personal scope, and the
honesty invariant.

**Proven:** 11 tests; **5 mutations, each verified to land** — a request-supplied `user_id` (reds the forgery
test), an open key set (reds the closed-set test), `create` instead of `firstOrCreate` (reds idempotency),
dropping the per-day filter (reds yesterday's-tick), dropping the self-only read filter (reds the personal
test). Idempotency is asserted at BOTH layers — the controller's `firstOrCreate` and the unique index itself,
so a future caller that forgets to guard still cannot double-write.

⚠️ **THREE ASSERTION FAULTS, ALL MINE, ALL THE SAME FAMILY.** `assertDontSee('is-ticked')` could never pass
because the layout's CSS rule `.vy-task-line.is-ticked` **ships** (§N.15.3, third time this programme) — the
needle became the space-separated class attribute, which is markup-only. And "All caught up" is also rendered
by the **notifications bell in the shell, on every page**, so both the DontSee *and* a positive assertion
elsewhere in the file were resolving against unrelated markup — the second one was **passing for the wrong
reason**. Needles are now scoped to the task card's own prose. Also: my fixture used `reported_at`/`property_id`
where the model has `opened_at` and derives the property from the unit.

Browser-verified as the demo operator: "0 of 3 ticked off" → ticked the urgent row → struck and dimmed, **"1
urgent" still legible beside it**, KPI card still "3 · 1 urgent", progress "1 of 3"; a double-POST wrote ONE
row. Fixture reverted — 0 ticks, 3 open work orders, identical to the pre-pass snapshot.

**Untouched:** the derived task computation · the housekeeping/availability system · other dashboard cards ·
isolation/RBAC. **Logged, not built:** `D1-2` (the category dimension + a persisted grouping preference) is the
natural next item and shares this table's shape. Suite **2251 / 2242**, 14,434 assertions, 6 non-green = the
documented set; PHPStan L5 (0); Pint clean.

## 2026-08-15 — D1-2 · grouping the dashboard tasks by category (a personal, persisted arrangement)

⚠️ **THE CONFIRM STEP CHANGED WHAT WAS BUILT, AGAIN.** The brief asked for a "grouping/collapse preference"
and framed the risk around a COLLAPSE hiding urgent work. The design register is explicit that the prototype's
control is **a two-button segmented switch between grouping by priority and grouping by category, persisted
across reloads** — there is **no collapse anywhere in it**. So none was invented: a collapse is precisely the
interaction that could hide urgent work, and building one the design never asked for, to guard a risk the
design never takes, would have been inventing UI. **Logged, not built.**

⚠️ **BUT THE INVARIANT IS REAL HERE — IN A DIFFERENT SHAPE, AND IT IS THE POINT OF THE PASS.** Grouped by
PRIORITY, urgency *is* the section heading. Grouped by CATEGORY it is not — so re-arranging the list would
have quietly buried which work is urgent, the same harm in the form this feature can actually take. The fix
travels with the data: each category section carries its **real urgent count** and every row keeps its own
priority mark (`aria`-named, not colour-only). Both halves are mutation-proven, and a test resolves the real
work to show the signal clears **while the preference stays** — governed by counts, never by a setting.

⚠️ **A SIBLING TABLE, NOT A ROW IN `operator_task_states` (§N.27.4).** The two share a discipline — personal,
generated NOT NULL key, unique, self-only — but not a KEY: a tick is scoped to a **day** (so yesterday's tick
cannot suppress today's task), while a display preference must **outlive the day**. Reusing that table would
have meant a sentinel date or a grouping that silently reset every midnight. Same shape, different lifetime;
the shape is mirrored, the table is not. Both key columns are NOT NULL, so the unique index genuinely applies
(the NULL-inert lesson, third application).

⚠️ **THE CATEGORY IS DERIVED, NOT STORED TWICE.** `work_orders.urgent` → `work_orders`, read from D1-1's own
key namespace via `OperatorTaskState::categoryFor()`. A new task type therefore cannot arrive with a key but
no category, and a test asserts every key in the closed set resolves to a NAMED label — an unlabelled one
would have rendered a heading like "Work_orders".

**Built:** `operator_dashboard_preferences` (unique on org+user → idempotent at the database) · the
category derivation + labels on the model that owns the keys · a `grouping` action on D1-1's existing
self-only controller (same route group, same discipline) · the segmented control · the urgent-count chip and
per-row priority mark.

**Proven:** 13 tests; **5 mutations, each verified to land** — removing the section's urgent chip and removing
the per-row priority mark each red the invariant (the two halves are independent); making the preference
shared reds the personal test; a request-supplied `user_id` reds the forgery test; opening the value set reds
the closed-set test. Also pinned: an unknown STORED value falls back to the default rather than rendering a
grouping the view has no branch for, and D1-1's ticks still work under the new grouping.

⚠️ **THE §N.15.3 TRAP, FOURTH TIME — AND THIS TIME IT WAS MY OWN NEW CSS.** `assertDontSee('vy-task-sec-urgent')`
could never pass because the rule I had just added to the layout ships with the page; worse, the matching
`assertSee` was partly passing on the stylesheet rather than the markup. Both needles are now the class
ATTRIBUTE (`class="vy-task-sec-urgent"`), which only exists in rendered markup. Separately, a count pinned
from the DEMO database ("7 to clean") failed against a fixture with one task — **a constant copied from
another environment is not an assertion about this one.**

Browser-verified as the demo operator: priority headings + the switch → clicked Category → headings became
Arrivals / Housekeeping / **Work orders with a "1 urgent" chip**, every row keeping its priority dot and real
count; a fresh page load came back still on Category. Fixture reverted — 0 preferences, 0 ticks, 1 urgent
work order, identical to the pre-pass snapshot.

**Untouched:** `tasks()`'s derivation (the output is grouped, the counts are not recomputed) · D1-1's ticks ·
the other dashboard cards · isolation/RBAC. Suite **2264 / 2255**, 14,510 assertions, 6 non-green = the
documented set; PHPStan L5 (0); Pint clean.

## 2026-08-15 — D8-2 · a real turnover deadline in the housekeeping board's READY column

⚠️ **THE LEDGER SAID "no such column exists" AND SIZED IT M. THE REGISTER HELD THE BETTER ANSWER.** Its own
entry offered two routes — "a target-ready timestamp on `housekeeping_tasks`, **or derived from the arriving
reservation's check-in time + the property timezone**" — and closed with the rule that decided it: *"the
column is already there and honestly empty, which is the right holding state. **Do not fill it with a
guess.**"*

**DERIVED, and no column was added.** A room's deadline is the hour a guest may actually turn up, and the
product already knows that: the property's published `check_in_time`. So the target is shown **only where a
real, non-cancelled reservation arrives at THAT room on THAT date**, and it is **that room's own property's**
published time. Storing a `ready_by` would have been a second copy of a fact the schema already holds — free
to drift the moment a property changed its check-in hour (§N.8f).

⚠️ **THIS IS NOT A GUESS, AND THE DISTINCTION IS THE WHOLE PASS.** An estimated turnaround ("checkout + 90
minutes") would have been one. A published check-in time against a real booking is a fact: it is the moment
the room is contractually needed. Where either half is missing — no arrival, or no published time — there is
**no deadline**, and the column keeps the honest "—" it already had. Nothing rounds, estimates or defaults an
hour (#39; D1-3's coerced-time lesson).

**Reused, not invented:** the shared `App\Support\StayTime` — whose docblock already carries this rule
(*"an unset column returns NULL so the caller can OMIT the line rather than invent an hour"*) — in the board's
own 24h format, matching its existing started/completed labels.

⚠️ **ONE ARRIVAL MAP, SO TWO READERS CANNOT DISAGREE.** The board already resolved "who arrives at this unit
on this date" for the guest's VIP/preferences, but **dropped rows with no lead guest**. A second arrival query
for the deadline would have disagreed with the first: a booking with no lead guest is still a real arrival
with a real deadline. The map now keeps the RESERVATION and both readers derive from it — the guest lookup
behaves exactly as before (pinned by a test).

**Proven:** 11 tests; **3 mutations, each verified to land** — dropping the arrival requirement (every room
would get a "deadline"), defaulting a null time to 15:00 (D1-3's defect, exactly), and collapsing the
per-property lookup to one shared time.

⚠️ **THE THIRD MUTATION PASSED THE FIRST TIME, AND THAT WAS THE USEFUL RESULT.** With a single property in the
read set, `$checkInTimes[$task->property_id]` and `reset($checkInTimes)` are indistinguishable — the keying
that exists *because the board spans properties* was untested. A genuine two-property test was added (a second
property, its own room type/unit/task/booking, the context switched to "all" **through the real switcher
route**), and the mutation then reds. §N.4p: a guard is only proven by a mutation that can reach it.

⚠️ **TWO FIXTURE TRAPS, BOTH RECORDED IN THE CANON, BOTH WALKED INTO.** `book()` **hardcodes the reservation
header to 2026-09-01** — a `check_in` override reaches only the line — so the "arrival on a different date"
test silently created a same-date arrival and failed for the right reason on the wrong grounds; the TASK is
moved instead now. And `seedScenario`'s property publishes **no** check-in time (that is the demo seeder's
doing), so the populated case had to be constructed — the D1-3 inversion, one layer along: "populated on the
demo" says nothing about the world a test runs in.

Browser-verified on the demo: a real arrival today, one housekeeping task created for that room → the board
showed **"by 15:00" on room 103 (the row already flagged "Guest arriving today · VIP")** and an unchanged
"—" on all seven other rows. Fixture reverted — 7 tasks, check-in times untouched, identical to snapshot.

⚠️ **LOGGED, NOT FIXED — a defaulted hour elsewhere.** `OperatorNewReservation` falls back to a hardcoded
`'15:00'` when `check_in_time` is null (`:130`, `:242`) — the same class of invented time this pass refuses,
on a different surface. Out of scope here.

**Untouched:** the housekeeping system and its statuses · the elapsed/expected bar · the derivation's inputs ·
isolation/RBAC. Suite **2275 / 2266**, 14,542 assertions, 6 non-green = the documented set; PHPStan L5 (0);
Pint clean.

## 2026-08-15 — D23-2 · a domain tier on the permission matrix (display only)

⚠️ **THE BRIEF'S PREMISE WAS FALSE, AND THE CODE SAID SO.** The task described "a flat, hard-to-navigate
list". The matrix has grouped permissions by RESOURCE since it was built — `sections()` partitions on the key
prefix and the view renders a heading per group. The ledger's "aren't grouped" and the register's "the live
matrix groups by resource" disagreed; the code settled it. (§N.9's rule, again: verify a finding — including
one of our own — before acting on it.)

**But the gap is real, and measuring it showed why:** **49 permissions under 30 resource headings, 20 of them
holding exactly one row.** Grouped in name, flat to the eye. So the build is the coarser tier the design
actually asks for — **Operations · Guests · Finance · System & access** — above the resource headings.

⚠️ **THE OTHER HALF STAYS REFUSED, ON THE DESIGN PASS'S OWN ARGUMENT.** D23-2 also wants friendly capability
names, and that was refused with a reason that still holds exactly: *"Manage team & roles"* conflates
`users.manage` **and** `roles.manage` — **the two tiers gating this very page**. Blurring two permissions on
the screen that grants them is a correctness risk, not a copy improvement. Every row keeps its 1:1
key-derived label; only the headings above them changed. A test asserts the two keep separate rows in
separate sections and that the conflated phrase never appears.

⚠️ **PARTITIONED, NOT FILTERED — the guard the whole pass rests on.** An admin cannot grant what they cannot
see, so a grouping that silently drops a permission removes a capability from the product's reach. The test
compares the grouped set against the **catalogue the matrix itself publishes** (never a pinned number): same
set, each key exactly once. An unmapped resource falls to **"Other"**, which is in the display order — so a
permission added tomorrow appears rather than vanishing.

**Display only, and structurally so:** the domains are a VIEW TRANSFORM built in the component from the same
`sections` list, not a second list shipped alongside it — there is one source of truth and no way for the two
to disagree about which permissions exist. `catalogPermissions()`, `permLabel()`, `save()` and the
spatie-teams checks are untouched.

**Proven:** 7 tests; **3 mutations, each verified to land** — an unmapped resource escaping the ordered
domains, a whole domain filtered out of the sections, and a permission duplicated into two groups. Plus a test
that a saved grant still genuinely authorises through spatie (team-pinned), so the grouping changed no
behaviour.

⚠️ **THE BROWSER CHECK THAT MATTERED MOST WAS A NO-OP SAVE.** Re-grouping the markup could have dropped
`permissions[]` inputs — and because the save DIFFS against the DB, a dropped input does not fail loudly, it
**silently revokes**. Saving a role unchanged and confirming the pivot stayed at 250 (Group Admin still 42, 49
permissions) proves the regrouped form still submits the complete set, and left the demo untouched.

⚠️ **THREE INSTRUMENT SLIPS, ALL MINE.** The page 403'd as `demo-staff` — this screen needs `roles.manage`,
so the pass had to run as `demo-admin` (§N.14.1: a render pass is bounded by the ROLE it runs as). A `can()`
asserted outside the spatie TEAM context answers for no team and reads as revoked. And "System & access"
reaches the page through `Js::from`, which escapes the ampersand to a unicode escape and then escapes THAT
backslash again for its `JSON.parse('…')` wrapper — two hand-written needles missed it silently before the
assertion was changed to **derive** the payload the same way the view does.

Rendered as the Property Owner: four domain headings, 30 resource sections beneath them, **49 permission rows
— the exact catalogue count**. RBAC state identical to the pre-pass snapshot.

**Untouched:** the permission catalogue · the labels · the role→permission grants · the spatie-teams
enforcement · `organization_id` isolation. **Not built:** `D23-3` (roles as a card grid) — the register keeps
it as its own gate because it restructures the page's three-column shape. Suite **2282 / 2273**, 14,721
assertions, 6 non-green = the documented set; PHPStan L5 (0); Pint clean.

## 2026-08-16 — D18-6 · the rate-plan list says which room type it prices (D18-5 stays a founder call)

⚠️ **THE PAIR DOES NOT BUNDLE, AND THE BUILDABLE ONE IS THE OPPOSITE OF THE BRIEF'S ASSUMPTION.** The task
proposed doing D18-5 and logging D18-6. Reading both entries reverses it:

- **D18-5 — NOT BUILT, and it is not a shape change.** The grid's rows are room TYPES because `rate_calendar`
  is keyed on `rate_plan_id` and a rate plan belongs to a room type. Per-unit rows would require **per-unit
  rate plans** — a pricing-model change carrying a genuine product question the register already names:
  *should two units of the same type be priceable apart?* That is a founder decision (STRUCT-1), not a
  display item, and the safeguard is already in place: the row's sub-label states how many physical units a
  save touches, so nobody is misled about what they are pricing. **Logged, unchanged.**
- **D18-6 — BUILT.** A real clarity defect on the screen that sets prices.

⚠️ **THE DEFECT, AND IT WAS BIGGER THAN RECORDED.** The plan list rendered only a name and a meta line, and a
rate plan belongs to a room type — so plans of the same name were **word-for-word identical**. The register
found two "Flexible" plans; the live demo has **THREE** (Double Room, One-Bedroom Apartment, City Studio).
§N.27.1 again: a register is one reader's finding. The derived rows were ambiguous in the same way — "−10% ·
derived from Flexible" does not say *which* Flexible. Each row now carries its room type.

**Read payload + display only.** `with('roomType:id,name')` on the existing query, one field on the payload,
one composed line in the view. No rate value, no derivation, no pricing computation, no VAT, nothing from
§G.1 was touched — and it is **proven, not asserted**: `rate_calendar` measured **929 rows / 10,920,000 minor
before and after, byte-identical**, plus a per-test JSON comparison of the whole table around a render.

**Proven:** 6 tests; **3 mutations, each verified to land** — dropping the room type (restores the original
defect), hardcoding it (proves it is READ, not invented), and printing a lone separator for an empty label.

⚠️ **A TEST WAS RETIRED FOR PRETENDING.** The dangling-separator edge test deleted a room type and asserted no
stray "·" — but a plan is only listed when its room type is in the grid's loaded set, so deleting the type
removes the PLAN too and the empty-label branch never renders. The mutation that printed a lone separator
**passed that test happily**. It was replaced with the reachable truth (the listed set is exactly the plans
whose type is in scope), and the `?? ''` stays as cheap null-safety rather than a guarded behaviour. §N.4p: a
guard is only proven by a mutation that can reach it.

⚠️ **THREE INSTRUMENT CORRECTIONS, ALL WORTH KEEPING.** (1) **`Livewire::test` renders no plans at all** here —
the grid scopes on the PROPERTY CONTEXT, which HTTP middleware resolves, so a component test mounts with an
empty read set (#20's shape, one layer along); the assertions go through the rendered page. (2) **Livewire
injects `<!--[if BLOCK]-->` markers around every `@if`**, which split the composed line in the delivered HTML
— invisible on screen, fatal to any reader of the rendered text; the view now prints ONE expression instead
of wrapping a directive round the label. (3) `setRate`'s range is **half-open**, so `start === end` writes
nothing and reads exactly like a broken fixture; and the column is `price_minor`, not the `rate_minor` a
first guess reaches for.

Browser-verified as the operator: the two "Flexible" rows now read *"Double Room · Free cancellation…"* and
*"One-Bedroom Apartment · Free cancellation…"*, and the derived rows name their type as well. Rate money
identical to the pre-pass snapshot.

**Untouched:** the rate values · the derivation engine · the pricing computation · the VAT-inclusive tiers
(§G.1) · isolation/RBAC. Suite **2288 / 2279**, 14,742 assertions, 6 non-green = the documented set; PHPStan
L5 (0); Pint clean.

## 2026-08-16 — DO24-1 · the owner's full statement archive as one ZIP

The Archive page's "Download ZIP" was an honest disabled control — there was no builder. There is now.

⚠️ **THIS IS BULK EGRESS, SO THE SCOPE IS THE FEATURE, NOT A DETAIL.** One request now emits many documents,
which turns a scoping slip from "one wrong page" into a bulk leak. Three boundaries hold it, and each is
mutation-proven:

- **THE ROWS** — the query is `OwnerStatement::query()->archived()`, carrying the owner + organization global
  scopes. No status or owner predicate is hand-written; the set comes from the **same shared scope the
  Archive PAGE reads**, so the bundle cannot contain more (or less) than the list it claims to bundle. Two
  `whereIn`s for one concept is exactly how a download and its page drift apart (§N.8f).
- **THE GATE** — the route sits in the existing `CAP_EXPORTS` group, the same capability gating every
  individual statement PDF. Bundling must never become a way around the gate on downloading one.
- **THE CONTENTS** — each PDF is built by the SAME `OwnerStatementDocument::data()` and the SAME per-owner
  `CAP_PAYOUT` check the single download uses, so **the #28 rule travels INTO the zip** rather than being
  re-decided at its edge: an accountant may export the archive and still never receives an account number.

**Read-only** (the only row written is the export audit), **one audit stamp per bundle** whose watermark goes
on every page of every document inside, and the temp file is deleted after send. **Synchronous, deliberately:**
an archive is one statement per period — tens of documents, and the page states the count before the click.
PDFs are rendered one at a time straight into the zip on disk, never all in memory. ⚠️ A queued build + signed
link is the next step **if** archives outgrow a request; logged, not built.

⚠️ **`ext-zip` IS NOW DECLARED IN `composer.json`** — the first hard extension dependency this repo takes. It
is present everywhere in practice, but depending on it silently would mean an owner discovering its absence
at download time instead of the deploy discovering it at install time.

**Proven:** 9 tests, **every content assertion OPENS THE REAL BYTES** (unzip, read the entries) rather than
trusting a 200; 3 mutations, each verified to land — dropping the owner/org scope (another owner's statements
appear in the bundle), dropping the payout check, and skipping cleanup.

⚠️ **THE MUTATION THAT EXPOSED A VACUOUS TEST.** The first #28 test searched the zip bytes for the IBAN
digits — but a PDF compresses its streams and the zip compresses again, so that needle can **never** match
whether or not the number is there. Forcing `canSeePayout = true` passed it happily. It was replaced with a
**differential** test that holds everything constant (same accountant, same statement, same watermark) and
varies only whether a payout account exists: if the check is honoured, an account the accountant may not see
cannot change a single byte of their archive. That version reds under the mutation.

⚠️ **TWO MORE INSTRUMENT LESSONS.** (1) **A single-file test run hides helper collisions** — this file's
`archiveOwner()` duplicated one in `OwnerArchiveViewTest`, passing alone and FATALLY redeclaring in the full
suite; renamed, and the reason recorded where the next person will read it. (2) `sequence_no` **restarts per
owner**, so two owners' first statements for the same month produce byte-identical filenames — harmless in
production (an archive holds one owner's documents) but it made "B's file is absent from A's zip" unprovable
by name until B was given distinct periods.

⚠️ **AN ANOMALY RECORDED AS UNEXPLAINED (§N.18.6).** One full-suite run showed a 7th non-green
(`OperatorSearchTest`). It passes alone (13/13), touches nothing this pass changed, did not reproduce on a
second full run, and a **stashed clean-worktree run showed the documented 6** — so it is intermittent, not
this change. Noted rather than explained away.

Browser + real HTTP as the demo owner: the control reads "One ZIP of 6 statement PDFs" (matching the six
statements listed above it), and the downloaded file unzips to **six real `%PDF-1.7` documents** named per
statement. Fixture cleaned — temp files removed, the two audit rows my downloads wrote deleted, demo data
identical to the pre-pass snapshot.

**Untouched:** statements, lines, payouts and every other export · `organization_id` isolation · RBAC · the
#28 perimeter. Suite **2297 / 2288**, 14,784 assertions, 6 non-green = the documented set; PHPStan L5 (0);
Pint clean.
