## 2026-08-16 — D4-1 · the operator Reports Excel workbook (and the spreadsheet-library decision)

The Reports export menu offered PDF and CSV, with "Excel workbook" disabled and honestly captioned *"Needs a
spreadsheet library — coming soon"*. That caption was accurate: **the gap was a dependency, not a build.** It
is closed.

⚠️ **THE LIBRARY CALL — `openspout/openspout`.** The ledger's own note suggested `phpoffice/phpspreadsheet`,
and `maatwebsite/excel` is the reflexive Laravel answer. Both were rejected for concrete reasons:
PhpSpreadsheet holds the entire sheet in memory, which is the exact ceiling an export must not have; and
maatwebsite 3.x pins `illuminate/*` constraints, i.e. it couples an export format to the framework's major
version — a poor trade on Laravel 13, which is already ahead of most packages. OpenSpout writes each row
straight to disk with **no framework coupling at all**. The claim was measured, not assumed: **12 MB at 10,000
rows and 12 MB at 100,000 rows** — flat, on a 128 MB limit.

⚠️ **ONE SURFACE, DONE PROPERLY — AND THE OTHER ONE DELIBERATELY LEFT.** Two Excel gaps are on the register:
this one and `D12b-1` (Maintenance Costs). Adding both in one sweep would have been the same mistake as
forcing an unrelated pair into one bundle: a different scope, different columns and a different gate
(`maintenance.manage`) do not become one job because they share a file extension. `D12b-1` is logged as
**unblocked ordinary work** — the shared writer is there for it — and left for its own confirm pass.

⚠️ **THE EXPORT *IS* THE VIEW, AND THAT IS ENFORCED BY THERE BEING ONE OF IT.** The load-bearing risk with any
export is that it quietly re-queries the table: it then hands the operator rows their screen may not show them
(a leak) and rows their filter excluded (a lie about what they were looking at). The CSV's scope + period
resolution was therefore **extracted into a single private `view()`** that the CSV and the workbook both read.
Neither export owns a predicate. A month filter exports that month because there is nowhere else for the
period to come from (§N.8f).

⚠️ **THE CELLS ARE TYPED — THE ONLY REASON A WORKBOOK BEATS A CSV.** A workbook that writes "€1,234.56" as a
STRING is strictly worse than the CSV beside it: it looks correct and then refuses to SUM, the single thing a
person opens a workbook to do. So money is a NUMBER with the currency in the cell's number format, months are
DATE cells (a stringified "Apr" sorts before "Aug" alphabetically and is wrong every year), shares are percent
cells. ⚠️ **Nothing is re-priced** — the integer minor amount is the one the screen renders (VAT-inclusive,
§G.1); this changes its TYPE, never its value, and a test pins the workbook's sum against the screen's own
breakdown to the cent.

**Verified by opening the real file, never by a 200.** A live download as the demo operator produced a genuine
`Microsoft Excel 2007+` file whose raw XML shows revenue cells with no `t=` attribute (numeric: `6340`) and
month cells carrying date serials (`46023`), with number formats `"€"#,##0.00` and `mmm yyyy`; read back
through a reader the columns are `int`/`float`/`DateTimeInterface`; and its channel figures sum to €7,080.00,
exactly what the page displayed. Filtering to `?month=2026-03` returned **one** month row whose value matched
that month in the full-year file — a real subset, not the table.

⚠️ **A MUTATION THAT WOULD NOT RED, CHASED TO GROUND RATHER THAN SHRUGGED OFF (§N.4p).** Six mutations were
applied and each verified to land. Dropping the period filter reds the reflects-the-view test; dropping the
property scope reds the property test; stringifying money reds five tests at once. But **removing the tenant
scope did not red the cross-org test — and neither did removing the property scope AND the tenant scope AND
the breakdown's own scope.** The reason is real defence in depth: the org boundary on this path is enforced
independently at the property-id set (org-scoped by `PropertyContext`), the `reservations` global scope, and
the tenant scope on the folio rows the money is summed from — the revenue itself is unreachable cross-org.
Rather than leave a test that credits a guard it cannot exercise, the cross-org test was made to **prove its
own premise**: it reads the RAW `folio_items` table to pin that €1,290 genuinely exists and is genuinely
leakable, then asserts the workbook carries €300. The limitation is written into the test where the next
person will read it.

**Untouched:** the on-screen Reports page and its figures · the existing CSV (a test pins its unchanged
formatted-string shape) · the PDF · `organization_id` and RBAC (same `reports.view` gate as the page it
exports) · §G.1 money values. No import path was added.

⚠️ **BASELINE NOTE.** The suite shows 9 non-green against a documented 6. `BookingImportTest` passes alone
(in-suite ordering, the documented one); `OwnerUnitDetailViewTest` and `PhaseBEndToEndTest` fail **identically
on a stashed clean worktree**, so they are pre-existing and date-sensitive (today's date rolled during the
session), not this change. Recorded rather than absorbed into the band.

Suite **2307 / 2298**, 14,855 assertions; PHPStan L5 (0); Pint clean.

## 2026-08-16 — the invented `'15:00'` on the New Reservation form (D8-2 follow-up)

D8-2 established the rule on the housekeeping board: **a time is a fact or nothing.** `ready_by` derives from
the property's published `check_in_time`, and an unpublished time yields *no deadline* — never `by 00:00`. It
logged the New Reservation form as carrying the same defect. It does, and now it does not.

⚠️ **THE REGISTER UNDER-DESCRIBED IT — AGAIN (§N.27.1).** It named "two sites in `OperatorNewReservation`".
The file is `app/Livewire/Operator/NewReservation.php`, and the form carried **four** inventions:

1. `:130` — the post-create confirmation panel: `'15:00'` when the property published nothing.
2. `:242` — the house-rules panel: the same `'15:00'` …
3. `:243` — …and, **one line below it, an identical `'11:00'` for check-out**, which the register never
   mentioned and which it would have been incoherent to leave: the same function, half-honest.
4. The **view**, `new-reservation.blade.php:363-364` — `?? '15:00'` / `?? '11:00'` sitting downstream of (2)
   and (3). ⚠️ This one matters most: fixing the component alone would have changed nothing a user sees,
   because the view would have re-fabricated exactly the value the component had just made honest. A fix that
   stops at the first layer is not a fix.

⚠️ **THE BLAST RADIUS TURNED OUT TO BE THE EASY PART, AND CONFIRMING IT CHANGED THE FIX.** The brief allowed
for storing the real published time if a NOT NULL consumer needed one. Reading the schema settled it: **the
form writes no time at all** — `reservations` carries `date('check_in')` and has no time column (a test pins
that with a raw `SHOW COLUMNS`). Both sites are purely presentational, so null-safe is unambiguously correct
and nothing downstream can break. D8-2's board reads the same `properties.check_in_time` independently and is
untouched.

**The fix reuses D8-2's source of truth rather than inventing a second convention (§N.8f):** `App\Support\
StayTime::display()`, whose docblock already documents this exact defect class ("a fabricated fact that
happens to match, which is the kind that survives review") and which returns NULL precisely so a caller can
omit rather than invent. It also replaced `substr((string) $time, 0, 5)`, which is not a safe way to read a
time. Absence renders as: the confirmation sentence **drops the "from HH:MM" clause entirely**, and the
house-rules rows show **"—"**, the idiom that panel already uses for an unset minimum stay. ⚠️ Never `00:00`,
which is simply a different lie.

⚠️ **EVERY FIXTURE PUBLISHES A NON-15:00 TIME (14:00 / 10:30) — the D8-2 M3 lesson.** On a 15:00 property the
invention and the fact are indistinguishable and a restored `'15:00'` passes happily. Three mutations, each
verified to land, each redding its own site independently: restoring `'15:00'` at `:130` reds the
confirmation-panel absence test; restoring the pair at `:242` and restoring the view's `??` defaults each red
the house-rules absence tests. ⚠️ Recorded precisely: the *flow-through* assertions do **not** red under those
mutations, because the published path was already correct — they are non-regression guards, not proofs of the
fix. ⚠️ And the assertions read **rendered markup, never source**: the fix leaves "15:00" in explanatory
comments, and a source-scanning guard would read its own needle (§N.27.5).

**Verified live, both branches.** As the demo operator the panel still reads *"From 15:00 · By 11:00"* —
byte-identical to before, **because on the demo that is now a FACT rather than a coincidence**, which is
exactly why the bug survived this long. Blanking the published times re-rendered it as *"— · —"*. ⚠️ The demo
DB was then restored to the seeder's `15:00:00`/`11:00:00` and raw-query verified on both properties.

⚠️ **LOGGED, NOT FIXED — the same anti-pattern in two other places** (different realms and surfaces, each
deserving its own confirm pass rather than a blind copy of this one): `GuestCheckinController::timeLabel()`
returns `'15:00'` for an absent or unparseable time — a **guest** told to arrive at an hour nobody published,
which is the higher-stakes instance — and `emails/pre-arrival.blade.php:65` defaults `?? '15:00'` /
`?? '11:00'` in the pre-arrival email.

**Untouched:** the reservation-create flow · D8-2's board and `ready_by` (its tests re-run green) · the

## 2026-08-16 — D12b-1 · the Maintenance Costs workbook (the D4-1 recipe, re-applied)

The Costs export menu offered PDF and CSV with "Excel · coming soon (use CSV)". D4-1 paid the library fork, so
this was ordinary work: reuse `App\Support\Export\Workbook` (openspout) **as-is**, no re-fork, no
investigation.

⚠️ **THE RESOLVER ALREADY EXISTED — AND SAID SO.** Unlike D4-1, this controller's private `scope()` was
already the shared reading of property scope + period, with a docblock recording the exact drift bug it was
created to prevent (the screen reading `?period=` while the export read `?from=`/`?to=`). Reusing it was the
whole job: the workbook owns no predicate, so a chosen period exports that period because there is nowhere
else for the period to come from. Same `maintenance.manage` gate and same audit as its siblings.

⚠️⚠️ **CONFIRM-FIRST CAUGHT A REAL TRAP, AND IT CHANGED THE BUILD.** The brief asked that the summary tab
reconcile to the line-item tab. Reading the service first showed it *could not*: `report()` sums `cost_minor`
over **every** resolved ticket in the window, while `billable()` carried `->limit(60)`. That is entirely
reasonable for a screen preview and a **defect in a workbook** — above 60 tickets the Summary tab would
silently exceed the detail printed beneath it, and a workbook is exported precisely to hold the whole detail.
Asserting equality blindly would have encoded the bug; removing the cap globally would have changed the
screen.

`report()` therefore gained an **optional detail depth**: the default is the unchanged 60-row preview (the
page, the CSV and the PDF are byte-for-byte unaffected — pinned by a test) and the workbook passes `null` for
the complete set. Same resolver, same scope, same period; only the depth differs. ⚠️ **The reconciliation test
creates 63 tickets on purpose** — with three it would pass whether or not the cap had ever been addressed.

⚠️ **PRE-EXISTING, LOGGED NOT FIXED:** the **CSV** has the same shape — a reconciling totals row printed under
a silently capped 60 rows, with nothing on the artifact saying the detail is a preview. Not touched here (the
brief was one page, and changing an existing export's contents is its own decision), but it is a real
"no silent caps" instance and is now written down.

⚠️ **HONEST LIMIT ON "LARGE-SAFE", MEASURED RATHER THAN CLAIMED.** The *writer* is O(1) — D4-1 measured it
flat at 12 MB for both 10k and 100k rows. But lifting the cap means the *source* materialises the period's
rows, which is linear: **5,000 line items measured at a 16 MB delta, 80.5 MB peak** — comfortable against the
suite's 512 MB, and far beyond any real operator's resolved work orders in one window. It is bounded, not
unbounded, and a chunked read would remove the ceiling entirely: logged, not built. Claiming end-to-end O(1)
here would have been false.

⚠️ **A FLOAT ASSERTION THAT WAS TESTING IEEE-754, NOT THE EXPORT.** Summing 63 exact `minor ÷ 100` cells drifts
by ~1e-13, so the detail sum and the summary cell differ in the last bits — as Excel's own `SUM()` does. The
assertion was corrected to compare **to the cent**, which is what #17 means; comparing binary floats for
identity would have been a false failure dressed as rigour.

**Verified by opening the file, never a 200.** A live download as the demo operator produced a genuine Excel
file with tabs `Summary` and `Line items`; read back, work-order dates are `DateTimeInterface`, months are
date cells, money is numeric, and it reconciles: line items 45 + 180 = **225** = Summary "Total spend", with
by-category 180 + 45 and owner-billed 180 + operator-borne 45 both landing on the same 225.

**Five mutations, each verified to land, each redding its own guard:** dropping the period filter reds the
subset test; **restoring the 60-row cap reds the reconciliation test**; stringifying money reds four; dropping
`maintenance.manage` reds the RBAC test; dropping the property scope reds the scope test (unlike D4-1's
cross-org case, this one is *not* over-determined — the guard is genuinely load-bearing here).

⚠️ **A LEAK IN MY OWN D4-1 TEST HELPER, FOUND AND FIXED.** 117 orphaned temp workbooks had accumulated. The
**live path leaks zero** — a controlled before/after around a real download confirmed `deleteFileAfterSend`
fires — but the *test client never performs a real send*, so every test run littered a file. The D4-1 helper
copied the response file and unlinked only the copy. Both test files now unlink the original; a full suite run
leaves **0**.

**Untouched:** the on-screen Costs page and its figures · the CSV and PDF exports · D4-1's Reports workbook and
the shared `Workbook` helper · `maintenance.manage` / `PropertyContext` · §G.1 money values. No import path;
nothing re-priced. Demo fixtures restored (the two audit rows my live downloads wrote were deleted and
raw-verified at 0).

## 2026-08-16 — the suite's clock is frozen (date-fragile fixtures), and a correction to my own finding

⚠️ **FIRST, THE CORRECTION — THE TWO TESTS I NAMED AS DATE-FRAGILE ARE NOT DATE-FRAGILE.** The D4-1 and
D12b-1 reports recorded `OwnerUnitDetailViewTest` and `PhaseBEndToEndTest` as "pre-existing and
date-sensitive (today's date rolled during the session)". Running them under a frozen clock at 2026-06-15,
2026-08-16, 2026-09-15 and 2027-01-10 shows them failing **identically at every date**. They are
deterministically broken, not flaky. `PhaseBEndToEndTest` contains **no date reference at all**. I had
inferred a shared cause from the fact that both surfaced together on a clean worktree, and the inference was
wrong — the §N.27.1 lesson applied to my own ledger entry, not someone else's.

⚠️ **AND THE REAL PROBLEM IS AN ORDER OF MAGNITUDE LARGER THAN THE TWO NAMED TESTS.** Run with the clock at
**2027-03-04 the suite produces 52 failures across 25 files**; at the real date, 9. Nothing about the code
differs — only what day it is. Among the fragile files is `OperatorReportsWorkbookTest`, which **I wrote
three passes ago**. So the suite's baseline has been quietly meaning different things on different mornings,
and it would have become a scheduled-CI landmine the moment deployment made CI real.

**The cause is the PINNED direction, not the relative one.** Fixtures across the suite pin real dates in
September 2026 (`book()`'s `2026-09-01` and its many siblings) and then assert behaviour that depends on
those stays being **upcoming** — arrival windows, trips, "this month" occupancy, analytics ranges. The
fixtures never drifted; the present moved past them.

**THE FIX: one central frozen clock in `tests/Pest.php`** — `beforeEach` pins `Carbon` and `CarbonImmutable`,
`afterEach` clears them. Re-anchoring hundreds of fixtures across 25 files would have been a vastly larger and
riskier diff for the same result, and 18 files already set their own clock locally, which simply overrides
this one. ⚠️ **The anchor `2026-08-01 09:00:00` is deliberate, not "the day this was written":** it sits
inside a window proven stable by measurement (2026-06-01 · 2026-08-01 · 2026-08-16 · 2026-08-31 all green
across the previously fragile files, so it is not knife-edge) and before the September fixtures, so their
stays remain upcoming — which is what those tests assert.

⚠️ **THE DIFF IS ONE FILE. NO PRODUCTION CODE WAS TOUCHED** — a date-fragile test is a test defect, and
changing the code under test to satisfy a flaky test would have been a new defect.

⚠️ **IT MAKES NOTHING PASS THAT WAS FAILING.** Frozen, the full suite reproduces the **same 9 non-green, the
same identities, the same 2,324 tests and 14,938 assertions** as the unfrozen run on the same day. The
documented non-green set is therefore **unchanged** — those 9 were never date-related, which is exactly why
the correction above matters.

⚠️ **AND NOTHING WENT VACUOUS.** Two independent proofs. First, the tests demonstrably react to the clock —
if they ignored it they would have passed at 2027 rather than producing 52 failures. Second, a behaviour
mutation **under the frozen clock** (forcing `GuestTrip`'s `is_past` true regardless of date) reds 4 of 6
`GuestTripsTest` tests. Freezing fixed *which* clock they read, not *whether* they read one.

⚠️ **THE PROOF IS RE-RUNNABLE, DELIBERATELY.** `VY_TEST_NOW=2027-03-04 ./vendor/bin/pest` simulates a date
roll and overrides the anchor. It produced the 52 failures above; the override is kept so the next person can
verify the claim instead of trusting this entry.

⚠️ **LOGGED, NOT FIXED — the two genuinely broken tests**, now with their real causes rather than the wrong
one I recorded:
- `OwnerUnitDetailViewTest::it renders the unit's real facts…` — the fixture sets the unit
  `condition_status: 'out_of_service'` and then books it; the certified out-of-service path writes an
  availability block, so the booking throws *"Unit is blocked (inventory_block) over the requested dates."*
  A fixture that asks for two mutually exclusive states, failing at every date.
- `PhaseBEndToEndTest::it runs the full Phase B chain…` — *"Call to a member function all() on array"* inside
  `TestResponseAssert`. An assertion-shape error, entirely unrelated to dates.
Both are real correctness work with their own confirm pass; absorbing them into this one would have been
over-reach, and they are not flaky — they are consistently red, which is worse and easier to fix.

PHPStan L5 (0); Pint clean. Baseline **before**: 9 non-green at the real date, 52 at a rolled date.
**After**: 9 at any date.

## 2026-08-16 — D23-3 · the roles become a card grid

The register deferred this deliberately: it restructures the page's three-column shape, and folding a layout
change into an RBAC-sensitive surface is how a grant quietly disappears. It got its own gate, as intended.

**What changed, and only this:** the roles moved out of the 240px left column into a **full-width card grid**
above the page — a card per role carrying an icon tile, a selected tick, the name, the description, and a
level pill with the member count. The remaining page is **two columns** (matrix + a 300px rail) instead of
three, and the rail's "Selected role" card is now the **dark gradient hero** the design specifies.

⚠️ **THE "5 ACROSS" IS THE PROTOTYPE'S OWN RULE, NOT A HARDCODED COLUMN COUNT.** The prototype specifies
`repeat(auto-fit, minmax(190px, 1fr))`, which yields five cards at the design canvas and degrades instead of
overflowing. Measured in the browser: **5 columns at 1440px**, 6 at 1680px, 4 at 1280px. Pinning `repeat(5,
1fr)` would have matched the screenshot and broken every other width.

⚠️ **THE ICON IS KEYED TO THE ROLE'S REAL DERIVED `level`** — Admin / Manager / Supervisor / Team, which
`RolePermissionService::level()` computes from the role's ACTUAL grants. A card therefore cannot display an
authority glyph its permissions do not support, and the glyph moves the moment the grants do. An unrecognised
level falls back to the neutral tone rather than guessing a tier. The alternative — a per-role icon map — would
have been decoration asserting something the data does not say.

⚠️ **THE BLAST RADIUS WAS THE POINT, AND IT HELD.** D23-2's permission grouping shipped on this page days
ago; browser-verified after the restructure, all four domains still render (Operations · Guests · Finance ·
System & access) with all **49** permissions, the hidden `role` input still tracks the selection, CSRF is
intact, and clicking a card still drives both the matrix and the rail. The demo pivot is unchanged at
**250 / Group Admin 42 / catalogue 49** — the exact figures D23-2 recorded.

⚠️ **THE MUTATION THAT REFUSED TO RED, AND THE TEST IT EXPOSED.** The mandatory silent-revoke check —
renaming the form's `permissions[]` input — left the no-op-save test perfectly green. The reason is that the
test builds its payload in PHP and posts it, so it proves the **controller** round-trips a full set and says
nothing about what the **form** submits. On a form that DIFFS against the database, the input NAME is itself
load-bearing: rename it and every grant the form no longer carries is revoked on the next save, silently. A
second test now pins both carriers in the delivered markup — the checkbox **and** the hidden input that
preserves a locked-but-granted permission (the one an operator cannot see or toggle, and would therefore
never notice losing). Both mutations red against it.

**Four mutations, each verified to land:** slicing the role iteration reds the every-role test; renaming
`permissions[]` and deleting the hidden carrier each red the form-contract test; emptying the domain order
reds the D23-2 test.

⚠️ **A NEEDLE SLIP WORTH RECORDING, TWICE OVER.** Checking D23-2's survival in the browser first reported the
domains missing — they are **CSS-uppercased**, so `includes('Operations')` fails on rendered `OPERATIONS`.
And in the test, a per-role-name needle failed because `Js::from('Group Admin')` emits an entire
`JSON.parse('…')` expression rather than a bare quoted string; the whole role array ships as one payload, so
asserting that payload is both correct and stricter. Same class of trap D23-2 hit — derive the needle the way
the view writes it.

**Untouched:** the roles · the permission catalogue · the grants · spatie-teams enforcement · the two-tier
gate (a Front Desk operator still gets 403) · `organization_id` isolation. The diff is **one Blade file**
plus the new test; no PHP under test changed, and no role CRUD was added.

Suite **2332 / 2323**, 15,026 assertions; PHPStan L5 (0); Pint clean. Baseline unchanged: the same 9
non-green, all previously shown pre-existing.

## 2026-08-16 — the deployment-scoping pass (and a wrong PHP floor that would have failed the deploy)

The first pass of the deployment sprint: inventory what exists, rank the gaps by harm, build only the
highest-leverage artifacts. `docs/DEPLOYMENT.md` §0 and §7 are the deliverable.

⚠️ **THE BRIEF'S HEADLINE GAP WAS ALREADY CLOSED, AND CHECKING SAVED THE PASS FROM RE-DOING IT.** The GDPR
crontab was framed as the #1 undocumented risk. It is not undocumented: `docs/DEPLOYMENT.md` §1 has carried
the exact line, the consequence and a table of all 8 commands since 2026-08-08 (audit finding F6-4). The
scheduled list was re-derived from `php artisan schedule:list` rather than memory — **8 confirmed**, and
worth noting that `payouts:run` is among them, so a missing cron is a **financial** stoppage as well as a
legal one, which the existing framing under-states.

⚠️ **WHAT IS ACTUALLY MISSING THERE IS DETECTION, NOT DOCUMENTATION.** The failure mode is silence: no error,
no alert. A runbook cannot detect its own omission. That is why scheduler/queue **liveness alerting** ranks
second in the plan rather than "document the cron", which was already done.

⚠️ **THE REAL FIND — THE REPOSITORY'S DECLARED PHP FLOOR WAS WRONG, AND WOULD HAVE FAILED A CORRECTLY
FOLLOWED DEPLOY.** `composer.json` required `php: ^8.3`. The installed production graph requires **≥ 8.4.1**:
`openspout/openspout` (which **I added three passes ago in D4-1**) requires `~8.4.0 || ~8.5.0`, and the entire
`symfony/*` v8.1 stack requires `>= 8.4.1`. `composer why-not php 8.3.0` lists them. A server provisioned to
the floor this repository advertised — and which `CLAUDE.md` repeated — **could not install the application
at all**. It never surfaced locally because this machine runs 8.4.22.

This is the `ext-zip` lesson at a larger scale: a runtime requirement that is real but undeclared is
discovered by the deploy, not by the install. Fixed to `^8.4.1` (the exact floor, not a rounded `^8.4`, since
`symfony` needs `.1`), lock platform regenerated with **zero package version changes** (169 before, 169
after), `composer validate` clean, `check-platform-reqs --no-dev` fully green, suite unchanged.

⚠️ **AND A REQUIREMENT DELIBERATELY *NOT* DECLARED.** `ext-gd` is used by `PlaceholderImage` — but its only
callers are `DemoSeeder` and one test, and production is never seeded (§4). Declaring it would harden a
dev-only dependency into a production install requirement. A naive "grep found gd, declare it" would have
been wrong in the opposite direction; the requirement list is only useful if it is *exactly* right.

⚠️ **TWO CLAIMS I DECLINED TO MAKE AFTER CHECKING.** A raw grep says **121** `env()` keys are "missing" from
`.env.example` — a finding I did not report, because almost all are Laravel framework defaults that belong in
`config/` and were never meant to be listed. Filtered to Vyrobel's own config files the real number is **5**,
all optional-with-defaults (`HORIZON_*`, `PASSPORT_CONNECTION`, `STRIPE_TAX_BEHAVIOR`). And the audit's old
`SESSION_SECURE_COOKIE` gap is already closed. Separately, **zero `env()` calls exist outside `config/`**,
which is what makes the `config:cache` step in §5 safe — verified rather than assumed.

**The ranked plan (§7), by harm, each its own later pass:** 1 backups + a *proven restore* (the only
unrecoverable failure; an unrestored backup is a hypothesis) · 2 scheduler/queue liveness alerting · 3 a
deploy script (§5 is order-sensitive and hand-run) · 4 secrets management · 5 Dockerfile/pinned runtime ·
6 CI. The founder's Stripe/VAT/Passport/tax-rate flips are listed separately as **not** engineering gaps.

⚠️ **HONESTLY: THIS IS NOT "DEPLOY-READY".** What is DONE this pass is the inventory, the ranked plan, a
corrected PHP floor and a runtime-requirements section with a pre-flight command. What is PLANNED is
everything in §7 items 1–6. Nothing here has deployed anything.

**No application code was touched** — the diff is `composer.json`, `composer.lock` and the runbook. Suite
**2332 / 2323**, 15,026 assertions, the same 9 non-green as the previous three passes.

## 2026-08-16 — the dead `guest/partials/trip-card.blade.php`, deleted on proven absence

`DO-G1-1` / `DO-G10-4`: a Blade partial the register called dead code duplicating the live guest trip card.
It was. It is gone.

⚠️ **THE FILE ITSELF ARGUED IT WAS ALIVE.** Its docblock reads *"shared by Trips (and reused as the header on
the Reservation detail)"*, and it carries a `G10` accessibility comment from a later sweep — so it looks
maintained. Both are claims, not references. A content-based sweep edits dead files exactly as happily as
live ones, which is how a dead file accumulates evidence of life.

⚠️ **ABSENCE WAS PROVEN ACROSS EVERY MECHANISM, NOT ASSUMED FROM A NAME-GREP** — the thing a name-grep is
structurally blind to is the dynamic case, so each was closed separately: the dotted name
(`guest.partials.trip-card`), the slug, the slash path, `@include` / `@includeIf` / `@includeWhen` /
`@includeFirst` / `@each` / `@component`, `view()` / `View::make`, variable and string-concatenated view
names, `<x-…>` component-namespace registration, and any config array listing view names. **Zero references
in `app/`, `resources/`, `routes/`, `tests/`, `config/`** — every hit anywhere in the repo was a `docs/`
register entry about it, plus one unrelated test *comment*.

**Two facts made the verdict decisive rather than merely negative:**
- `resources/views/guest/` contains **no include directive of any kind** — not one `@include`, `@each` or
  `@component` in the entire realm. Nothing there can pull in a partial.
- The only genuinely dynamic renderer in the codebase, `PdfService::view($view)`, receives a **literal in
  every one of its nine call sites**, all under `pdfs.*`. It cannot resolve to a guest view.

⚠️ **AND THE RENDER CHECK WAS MADE NON-VACUOUS.** A page with no cards would survive deleting a card partial
regardless, so "200 OK" alone proves nothing. Re-rendered as the real demo guest after `view:clear` (a cached
compiled view can mask a broken reference), `/guest/trips` returns **two real trip cards** — `R-UAAXARVV`
and `R-KW3ASFRD`, 3 nights each, €369.00, "Paid in full" / "€184.50 due" — and the Reservation detail renders
too, both with zero view-not-found errors.

⚠️ **THE PROOF THEY HAD ALREADY DIVERGED**, which is the actual risk the register named: the deleted partial's
CTA read **"View booking →"**; the live card renders **"View reservation"**. Two implementations of one card,
already saying different words — a fix applied to one would silently have missed the other.

**Untouched:** the live trip card · the guest trip surfaces · every view include · the render pipeline.
`GuestTripsTest` 6/6 green after the deletion, which is what proves the surface outlived the file. Suite
**2332 / 2323**, 15,026 assertions, the same 9 non-green; PHPStan L5 (0); Pint clean.

## 2026-08-16 — the hand-rolled star colours become a token (DO10-4 closed)

⚠️ **THE PREMISE WAS WRONG IN A USEFUL WAY: THERE WAS NO STAR TOKEN TO MIGRATE TO.** The item read "replace
the hand-rolled star colours with the `--vy-*` design token". No such token existed. The tokens file carries
`--vy-amber`, `--vy-amber-2`, `--vy-amber-text` and `--vy-accent-3` — and `--vy-accent-3` is
`rgb(232,112,58)`, the **brand orange**, not the star gold `#8F5A06`. The only canonical star value in the
product was a **measured literal inside the shared component**, hand-copied into four more view files. So the
fix was to create the missing definition, not to point at one.

**`--vy-star: rgb(143,90,6)` and `--vy-star-empty: rgb(122,110,100)`** now hold the values — unchanged, still
the ones measured against the three real plates (peach `#FBD3BF` · owner card `#F8F4EF` · light card
`#FFFDFB`), empty always below filled so the hierarchy survives. The component reads them; the duplicates
were swapped.

⚠️ **THREE SWAPS WERE PARITY. ONE WAS A REAL COLOUR CHANGE, AND IT IS THE POINT OF THE ITEM.**
`owner/reviews:90`, `owner/reviews:123` and `operator/guest-profile:132` already held `#8F5A06`, so those are
pure de-duplication — not a pixel moved. But **`owner/reviews:163` was still painting `#E8A63A`**: the exact
gold the accessibility pass measured at **2.05** and rejected for missing the 3:1 a non-text graphic must
meet. It is a survivor of that fix — precisely the failure mode the original entry predicted ("a fix applied
to one silently misses the other"). Swapping it is a **visible change**, raised here rather than smuggled,
and it closes a measured contrast defect.

⚠️ **THREE THINGS DELIBERATELY LEFT, EACH FOR A DIFFERENT REASON:**
- **The review email** keeps its literal `#8F5A06`. Mail clients strip CSS custom properties; tokenising it
  would have broken the colour in most inboxes. Hand-rolling is *correct* there, and the token comment says so.
- **`guest/review` and `booking/room` / `booking/browse`** use `var(--vy-accent-3)` — a **ratified** choice,
  recorded in `guest/review.blade.php:46`: the component's old `#E8A63A` measured 2.05 on that page, so the
  orange was chosen deliberately and measured. Not a defect to "fix".
- **`owner/messages`' SVG stars** are message **flags**, not ratings. Same glyph family, different concept.

⚠️ **A 500 I CAUSED, AND THE TRAP BEHIND IT.** The first version of the token comment contained the component
tag `<x-star-rating>` written in angle brackets. **Blade compiles component tags anywhere in a file — CSS
comments included** — so the unclosed tag broke the whole tokens view and every page that includes it
returned a 500. A CSS comment is not a Blade comment, which is the same family as "CSS comments ship"
(§N.15.3), one layer deeper. Caught by rendering, invisible to `php -l`, and now warned about in the file
itself for the next editor.

⚠️ **AND THE CHANGE BROKE A REAL GUARD, WHICH THE SUITE CAUGHT.** `StarRatingCorrectnessTest` measures the
star inks by **reading them out of the rendered component** — its own comment records that asserting the hex
as a literal had been *vacuous*. Moving the colour into a custom property left no hex in that output, so the
contrast guard went blind and failed. Rather than weaken it, it now **follows the ink to its new home**:
assert the component defers to the token (and that no literal crept back beside it), resolve the token's real
value from the rendered token block exactly as a browser would, then run the identical contrast maths.
Mutation-proven twice — setting the token to the rejected `#E8A63A` reds it, and reverting the component to a
literal hex reds it too. The guard is **stronger** than before: it now protects the single definition and the
indirection.

**Verified by rendering, not by source:** on `/owner/reviews` the token resolves to `rgb(143,90,6)` and **all
20 star elements** compute to the filled or empty token — **none** remains at the old `rgb(232,166,58)`. The
operator and public realms both define the token too.

Suite **2332 / 2323**, 15,031 assertions, the same 9 non-green; PHPStan L5 (0); Pint clean.

## 2026-08-16 — DO20-1 · every PDF now carries "Page N of M"

The nine PDFs this product renders had no page numbering at all. `PdfService` already stamped a per-page
downloader watermark, so the per-page mechanism existed — the completeness mark did not.

⚠️ **WHY THIS IS NOT COSMETIC.** An unnumbered multi-page statement cannot be checked for completeness: page
3 of an unnumbered document is indistinguishable from the end of it, so a page lost in printing, scanning or
forwarding leaves no trace. On a financial document that is the difference between a reader knowing they have
all of it and assuming so.

⚠️ **IT COULD NOT BE DONE IN MARKUP, AND FINDING THAT OUT FIRST SAVED THE PASS.** The obvious approach — a
`{PAGE_NUM}` placeholder in the footer div the watermark already uses — **does not work in dompdf 3.x**: the
inline substitution in `Renderer/Text.php` is commented out, so the placeholder would have rendered
*literally*, on every page of every financial document. The working mechanism is the canvas page-script:
`CPDF::page_text()` registers a callback invoked once per page at OUTPUT time with the real
`(pageNumber, pageCount)`. **That is also what makes M the true total rather than a number this service had
to count for itself** — the denominator is supplied by the renderer after the document is laid out.

The stamp therefore lives in `PdfService::paginate()`, the ONE renderer all nine documents pass through
(§N.8f) — not in seventeen templates. It sits bottom-right, clear of the centred watermark, in the same
7.5pt / `#5f5853` so the two footer marks read as one family. The document is rendered explicitly first
(the page-script needs a canvas); the wrapper's own `rendered` flag stops that happening twice.

⚠️ **VERIFIED BY INFLATING THE REAL PDF BYTES — AND A ONE-PAGER WOULD HAVE PROVED NOTHING.** dompdf
compresses its content streams, so the text is unreadable until decompressed, which is precisely why
asserting on the HTML would have been worthless here: **there is no page number in the HTML at all.**
Fixtures were tuned to force genuine overflow, and the stamps read back exactly:

| pages | stamps found in the file |
|---|---|
| 1 | `Page 1 of 1` |
| 3 | `Page 1 of 3` · `Page 2 of 3` · `Page 3 of 3` |
| 4 | `Page 1 of 4` … `Page 4 of 4` |
| 6 | `Page 1 of 6` … `Page 6 of 6` |

The denominator moves with the document, which is the actual claim — a one-page test prints "1 of 1" whether
the logic is right or wrong.

**Also verified on a real document, not just the fixture:** the demo owner's statement PDF downloaded over
HTTP contains both `Page 1 of 1` **and** the downloader watermark (`Downloaded by Demo Owner … ·
Confidential`) — one footer mark did not evict the other. ⚠️ A first check reported the watermark missing and
was wrong: the parentheses in the emailed identity are backslash-escaped inside the PDF string, so the naive
pattern missed it. The mark was always there; the needle wasn't.

**Three mutations, each verified to land:** hardcoding the denominator to 3 reds the real-total test;
removing the stamp reds all four; skipping the explicit `render()` reds the multi-page tests (the single-page
case survives it, which is itself a reminder that only the overflow cases test the mechanism).

⚠️ **This is a SHARED change — all nine PDFs gained the footer**, which the item intended ("no page numbering
on *any* PDF"). No document's content or layout was restructured, and the full suite — including every
existing PDF test — is unchanged at the documented 9 non-green.

Suite **2336 / 2327**, 15,046 assertions; PHPStan L5 (0); Pint clean.

## 2026-08-16 — DO25-1 / DO23-2 · the §N.8f drift pair: both merges refused, the real risk guarded

Two items logged as "the same concern implemented twice". **They are two different drifts, so they were
split (the D18-5/D18-6 lesson), and both merges were REFUSED after reading all four sites.** A refusal that
shows its evidence is worth more than a merge that flattens something real.

⚠️ **DO25-1 — NOT ONE CONCEPT.** The register says the owner Reports chart is "a second implementation" of
`<x-charts.bars>`. It is not: the shared component is a **flex-column, single-series** chart with static
label rows; the Reports chart is **absolutely positioned**, carries a **prior-year ghost bar** layered behind
the live one, floats its value at the bar's top (`bottom:{pct}%` — it moves with the bar), and badges the
peak month with an inline star. Merging would mean adding a second layout mode inside a component with
**five working consumers** — a refactor beyond the drift, risking five surfaces to remove a duplication that
isn't one. ⚠️ Along the way a plausible-looking inference of mine was wrong: `<x-charts.bars>`'s `valueTop`
prop was added for the **operator** Reports page, not the owner one, so it is not evidence of an abandoned
migration.

⚠️ **DO23-2 — SAME LOOK, DIFFERENT INTERACTION MODEL.** Two day-cell families genuinely exist (`vy-cal-*`
and `vy-ud-*`), but Block Calendar **drag-selects a range** (`mousedown`/`mouseenter`/`aria-pressed`) and
POSTs a real block, while Unit Detail opens a **read-only detail popover**. Merging means parameterising two
300–450-line views by interaction mode. ⚠️ **And the cost this row was opened for has already been paid** —
the O10 keyboard lockout it cites was re-made on the second grid, and both now render real `<button>` day
cells with descriptive `aria-label`s and no clickable `<div>`. Verified by reading both. ⚠️ A first pass of
that check reported Block Calendar had no `aria-label`; that was **my grep**, not the code — the attribute
sits below the class on a later line and a single-line pattern missed it. Corrected before it reached a
verdict.

⚠️ **THE SWEEP FOUND THE REAL COST, AND IT IS FIVE TIMES BIGGER THAN EITHER ROW SAID.** Looking for the
duplication rather than at the two named files turned up **EIGHT bar implementations** — `components/charts/
bars`, owner `reports`, `dashboard`, `insights`, `unit-detail` (×2), `bookings`, and `statement` — every one
hand-carrying the same honesty rule: **a bucket worth zero must draw nothing.** That rule exists because the
Reports chart once applied a two-percent floor and five months that genuinely earned €0.00 each rendered a
visible bar, contradicting the figure printed beside them (#39). The fix then had to be copied by hand into
every other chart, and `statement` implements it a third way again (a `.is-zero` class resetting the floor).

**So the deliverable is the invariant, not a merge.** The layouts genuinely differ and flattening them would
be a new defect; the *rule* does not differ at all. `BarChartZeroFloorTest` now holds every implementation to
it — behaviourally for the shared component (render a zero bucket, assert no floor; render a real one, assert
the hairline IS applied, so it is a floor-for-nonzero rather than a blanket removal) and structurally for the
seven local charts, with Blade and CSS comments stripped first because several of those files *explain* the
floor in prose and a naive scan would have matched its own needle (§N.27.5).

**Three mutations, each verified to land:** restoring the floor in the shared component reds both the
behavioural and the structural test; losing the conditional in owner Reports (where the defect first shipped)
reds the structural one; deleting `statement`'s `.is-zero` reset reds the class-based one.

⚠️ **NOTHING WAS MERGED AND NO BEHAVIOUR CHANGED.** The diff is one new test file — no view, no component, no
data. Both sites of both items render exactly as before, which is the correct outcome when the copies are
genuinely divergent.

## 2026-08-16 — the two operator payout maps unified (§1.1 closed, and its headline was stale)

⚠️ **THE BRIEF SAID "TWO OPERATOR MAPS". THE REGISTER SAYS THREE, FLAGS IT 🔴, AND PUTS THE DANGEROUS ONE IN
THE OWNER REALM.** Reading §1.1 first changed what this pass was: three definitions of "payout status →
badge" — the owner shared trait plus a private copy inside each of `OperatorOwnerDetail` and `PayoutRun` —
and the owner copy's `default` arm badged `processing` and `held` as **"Payout pending"**, telling an owner
that money already in transit had not started moving.

⚠️ **AND THAT HALF WAS ALREADY FIXED — the register row is stale.** `FormatsOwnerData::payoutStatusMeta()`
now carries explicit arms: `processing` → **"In transit"**, `held` → **"On hold"** (DO-CORRECTNESS-1). Both
operator copies' docblocks even record the fix. So the money-misinformation defect this red row is named for
no longer exists; what remained was the duplication.

⚠️ **THE TRAP THIS PASS HAD TO AVOID: "unify to the shared source" WOULD HAVE MADE THINGS WORSE.** The
obvious §N.8f move is to fold the operator copies into the owner trait. That would have been wrong twice
over. Both components already documented why, and reading them confirmed it:

- **The tone vocabularies are disjoint.** The owner shell defines exactly three tone classes; the operator
  shell defines fifteen `tone-*` classes and defines **neither `paid` nor `draft`**. Feeding one realm's tone
  to the other's CSS yields an unstyled badge — the badge would lose its colour.
- **The realms speak differently on purpose.** An owner reads "In transit" and "On hold" about their own
  money; an operator reads the raw state. Collapsing them would have imposed one realm's voice on the other.

An existing test — `PayoutStatusLabelTest`'s third case — pins exactly that reasoning "so a later
'consistency' pass cannot collapse them without first disproving it". It is a guard on a **decision**, and it
did its job on me.

**So the unification is within the operator realm only.** The two copies were **byte-identical** (same four
arms, same `default => ucfirst($status)`), and both docblocks called the remaining duplication "a real,
narrower de-dup, logged rather than done". It is done: the map moved into `FormatsOperatorData`, the trait
**both components already used**, and both private copies were deleted — necessarily, since a class method
silently wins over a trait method and would have left the drift in place while looking fixed.

⚠️ **MONEY: BYTE-IDENTICAL, VERIFIED BOTH WAYS.** All six declared enum states plus an undeclared one were
captured through the old copies before the change and through the trait after: `pending`→Pending/pending ·
`processing`→Processing/departed · `paid`→Paid/confirmed · `failed`→Failed/no-show · `reversed`→Reversed/
cancelled · `held`→Held/departed · unknown→ucfirst/departed. Identical. Reflection then proves both
components resolve to **the same file AND the same line** (`FormatsOperatorData.php:374`) — the declaring
class alone proves nothing, because PHP flattens a trait into the using class. Both surfaces rendered as the
operator: owner-detail and payout-run each show `Paid · tone-confirmed` and `Pending · tone-pending`, matching
the seeded 5 paid / 1 pending exactly. The `payouts` table is untouched (5 paid €2,804.40 · 1 pending €885.60,
raw-verified identical before and after).

⚠️ **AN EXISTING GUARD BROKE, AND FOLLOWING IT WAS THE POINT.** `PayoutStatusLabelTest` asserted a
`private function payoutStatusMeta` inside each operator component — the shape the map had when the decision
was recorded. Deleting the copies failed it. The decision it guards is unchanged and still guarded; only the
mechanism moved, so the assertion now follows the map to its single home (same file, same line) and adds a
stronger clause: **no component may grow its own copy back**. Mutation-proven — re-adding a private copy reds
it.

**Three further mutations, each verified to land:** changing a label in the one map reds the parity test;
re-adding a private copy reds the one-source test; re-breaking the owner realm's `processing` arm reds the
realm-separation test.

⚠️ **NOT TOUCHED:** payout amounts, the payout computation, when `processing`/`held` are SET

## 2026-08-16 — DEPLOY §7.1 · backups, and a restore proven to reconstruct the data

Rank 1 of the deployment sprint: the only *unrecoverable* failure on the list. `ops/backup.sh` and
`ops/restore-drill.sh`, documented as §7.1 in the runbook.

⚠️ **THE RESTORE IS THE DELIVERABLE. THE BACKUP IS THE EASY HALF.** A script that produces a file proves only
that a file was produced — so `ops/restore-drill.sh` decrypts the archive, restores it into a **scratch
database**, and asserts the restored data matches the source: row counts for **all 130 tables** compared per
table (a total would let a +1/−1 cancel), field-by-field spot-checks on a reservation, a payout and a
statement, money totals (payouts · statement net · folio items), **270 foreign keys** restored with no
orphaned rows, and the file set by count plus a SHA-256 checksum.

⚠️ **AND THE DRILL FAILS IF THE SOURCE IS EMPTY.** An empty database restores perfectly and matches itself,
which is the DR version of a one-page PDF printing "1 of 1" — so the drill asserts the source has real
reservations before believing its own comparison. Proven on the real demo dataset: 41 reservations, payouts
totalling €3,690.00, folio items €9,200.40.

⚠️ **A DRILL THAT ALWAYS PASSES IS NOT A DRILL — SO IT WAS SHOWN TO FAIL.** A deliberately damaged archive (a
`reservations` INSERT block removed, the shape of a truncated dump) was fed to it: it reported
`✗ reservations: source=41 restored=0`, named the spot-check mismatch, and **exited 1**. The good archive
exits **0**. Both exit codes matter — they are what let cron or CI treat a failed restore as an alarm rather
than a log line nobody reads.

⚠️ **THE FINDING THAT WILL BITE SOMEONE LATER: `APP_KEY` GATES THE WHOLE BACKUP, AND IT IS DELIBERATELY NOT
IN IT.** Guest email/phone columns and the ID-document blobs are encrypted with it. **Without it, a restore
produces rows whose PII is permanently unreadable — the data is there and worthless. With it stored beside
the archive, the encryption protecting that PII is worthless instead**, because one stolen file would carry
both the ciphertext and its key. There is no version of this where the key belongs in the backup; it belongs
in a separate secret store, and losing it is as fatal as losing the backup. Written into §7.1 as a founder
step rather than solved silently.

⚠️ **THE BACKUP REFUSES TO RUN WITHOUT A PASSPHRASE** (exit 2, verified) rather than writing a tenant's entire
dataset in the clear — an unencrypted archive would be a GDPR breach committed by the backup itself. The
archive was checked as bytes, not assumed: `openssl enc'd data with salted password`, `Salted__` magic, and
**zero** plaintext PII strings recoverable from it. Retention (14 days, configurable) prunes **after** a
successful run, so a failed backup can never delete the last good archive.

⚠️ **A REAL RISK FOUND WHILE CLEANING UP: `storage/backups/` WAS NOT GITIGNORED.** The archive appeared in
`git status` as untracked — one `git add -A` from being committed, which would have put the entire tenant
dataset into the repository's permanent history, where a later key or passphrase leak would expose it
retroactively. `storage/` is not wholly ignored, so the directory needed its own rule. Added and verified
with `git check-ignore`.

**Safety of the drill itself:** it refuses outright if the scratch database name equals the source, and drops
the scratch schema on exit. Raw-verified afterwards — only `vyrobel` and `vyrobel_test` remain, and the
source still holds 41 reservations and €3,690.00 of payouts, byte-identical to before.

**No application code was touched** (the diff is `ops/`, `.gitignore` and the runbook), no dependency was
added — `mysqldump`, `tar` and `openssl` were already present — and the suite is unchanged at the documented
9 non-green.

⚠️ **HONESTLY, WHAT IS AND IS NOT DONE.** **DONE:** an encrypted, retained, schedule-ready backup of the
recoverable set, and a restore *proven* to reconstruct it, re-runnable by anyone. **STILL FOUNDER STEPS, and
§7.1 is not finished until they land:** an **offsite destination** — the archive currently lands on the same
machine it protects, which is no defence against disk loss or a compromised host — plus the `APP_KEY` and
passphrase secret store, and a recurring calendar slot for the drill. A backup that never leaves the box is
a real improvement and not yet disaster recovery.

## 2026-08-16 — DEPLOY §7.2 · the silence becomes audible (scheduler + queue liveness)

Rank 2 of the deployment sprint. §1 has documented the crontab correctly since the audit; **the gap was never
documentation, it was detection** — a runbook cannot detect its own omission. If cron stops, all eight
scheduled commands stop, including the **GDPR 14-day guest deletion**, the **30-day ID purge** and
**`payouts:run`**, and *nothing reports it*. No exception, no log line, no symptom until an erasure is legally
overdue or an owner was never paid.

⚠️ **THE COMMAND LIST WAS RE-DERIVED FROM `schedule:list`, AND IT SETTLED THE DESIGN.** All eight run
**daily** — so none of them can prove liveness at any useful resolution: a cron that died at 09:01 would look
identical to a healthy one until tomorrow. The heartbeats therefore run **every minute** and exist purely to
be observed; the real commands were not touched.

⚠️ **TWO HEARTBEATS, BECAUSE THEY FAIL SEPARATELY.** The scheduler stamps one directly; the queue's is
stamped inside `QueueHeartbeatJob::handle()` — **only a live worker reaches it**. Dispatching succeeds with
every worker dead (the row just sits there), so stamping at dispatch would make a dead Horizon look healthy
forever. A stalled scheduler with a fresh queue means cron; a fresh scheduler with a stalled queue means
Horizon. One combined signal could not tell an operator which to go and fix.

⚠️ **THE DETECTOR IS OUTSIDE THE THING IT WATCHES, WHICH IS THE WHOLE ARCHITECTURE.** A check running inside
the scheduler could never report the scheduler being dead — it would simply not run, which is
indistinguishable from healthy silence. So the app only **publishes** evidence at `GET /up/liveness`; the
alarm belongs to an external monitor polling it, and to the dead-man's-switch ping, which is the only
detector that survives power loss or a crashed host.

⚠️ **503, NOT A JSON FLAG.** Every uptime monitor alerts on a non-2xx; almost none parses a body. Returning
200 with `{"healthy":false}` would be a check that technically reports the outage while waking nobody — the
current situation with extra steps.

⚠️ **A HEARTBEAT THAT NEVER EXISTED COUNTS AS STALE, NOT HEALTHY.** Reading "no data" as "fine" would leave
the check silent in the exact case it was built for: a fresh deploy whose crontab line was forgotten.

⚠️ **AND ALERT FATIGUE IS ITSELF A FAILURE MODE** — a check that pages on one missed minute gets muted, and a
muted check restores the silence. Scheduler tolerates 5 minutes, queue 15 (a worker under load may defer a
low-priority probe). A blip inside tolerance stays silent, and that is tested.

**PROVEN BY FORCING EACH STALL, over HTTP against a live server** — an alarm nobody has triggered is
decoration: healthy → **200**; scheduler aged past its window → **503** *naming the scheduler while the queue
reads healthy*; queue aged past its window → **503** naming the queue; never-beaten → **503**; recovered →
**200**. `ops/liveness-drill.sh` re-runs all five and exits non-zero on failure.

**Four mutations, each verified to land:** treating a never-written heartbeat as healthy reds the
fresh-deploy test; returning 200 instead of 503 reds three; stamping the queue beat at construction reds the
round-trip test; dropping the beats to daily reds the cadence test.

⚠️ **A RESTORE THAT SILENTLY DID NOTHING, CAUGHT.** Reverting the third mutation with `git checkout` was a
no-op — the file is **untracked**, so git had nothing to restore, and the next mutation ran against a still-
mutated job (which is why its run showed an extra red). §N.4p applies to restores exactly as it applies to
mutations: verify the revert landed. Rewritten and re-verified, then M4 re-run cleanly.

**Untouched:** all eight scheduled commands (`schedule:list` still shows 8), their behaviour, and every
business path. The new code is confined to `app/Support/Ops`, `app/Jobs/Ops`, one route and two scheduler
entries — observation only, no dependency added.

⚠️ **HONESTLY, DONE vs FOUNDER.** **DONE:** the heartbeats, the endpoint, the drill, and an alarm *proven* to
fire on each real stall and stay quiet when healthy. **FOUNDER STEPS, and §7.2 is not finished without
them:** point an external uptime monitor at `/up/liveness` (unpolled, it is evidence nobody reads), optionally
set `OPS_HEARTBEAT_PING_URL` for the dead-man's-switch — **unset it is inert by design, and nothing pretends
otherwise** — and decide on-call routing. A working alarm wired to nobody is still silence.

Suite **2350 / 2341**, 15,171 assertions, the same 9 non-green; PHPStan L5 (0); Pint clean.

## 2026-08-17 — D18-5 · per-unit rate plans, PHASE 1 (founder ruling recorded) — and the question it exposed

⚠️ **FOUNDER RULING, recorded as what unblocked this:** two units of the same room type MAY be priced apart.
A rate may bind to a UNIT as an override, not only to a room type. D18-6 had left this as the open product
call; it is now made.

**BUILT — the foundation, and nothing that could misprice anything:**

- **`unit_rate_overrides`** — a NEW table, deliberately not a column on `rate_calendar`. Adding a nullable
  `unit_id` there would have altered the table every existing price lives in, and would have made its
  `UNIQUE(rate_plan_id, date)` depend on a nullable column — and **MySQL treats NULLs as distinct**, so that
  index would have gone quietly inert and allowed two conflicting type-level prices for one night (the
  DO-CORRECTNESS-1 waitlist lesson, this time on a money table). Every column of the new
  `UNIQUE(rate_plan_id, unit_id, date)` is NOT NULL; "applies to all units" is the ABSENCE of a row.
- **`NightlyRate`** — one resolver: a unit override wins, otherwise the type price, which is *exactly*
  today's behaviour. ⚠️ **That total fallback is the zero-movement guarantee**: the override table starts
  empty, so every resolution takes the old branch.
- **Reversible, zero-loss migration** — `down()` drops only the new table; `rate_calendar` is untouched in
  both directions.

⚠️ **ZERO PRICE MOVED, PROVEN ON THE WHOLE TABLE, NOT A SAMPLE.** `rate_calendar` hashes identically before
and after the migration — `2bbdafccc3b5c1ee43f89fe313a3f02d`, 929 rows, 10,920,000 minor — and the demo holds
**zero** overrides. §G.1, the VAT logic and the pricing computation were not touched.

⚠️⚠️ **CONFIRM-FIRST FOUND THE THING THE RULING DOES NOT SETTLE, AND IT IS WHY NO AUTHORING SURFACE SHIPPED.**
The brief assumed a single resolver to extend. There isn't one — **eight** call sites read `rate_calendar`
directly. More decisively, the real money path is `BookingEngineService::priceOver($ratePlanId, …)`: a stay is
priced **from a rate plan**, the folio is charged, and the **unit is assigned afterwards**. The guest
storefront therefore *cannot* consult a per-unit price, because at the moment money is taken **nobody has
chosen a unit yet**. The operator's New Reservation path *does* accept a `unit_id`, so it could.

**Shipping an authoring surface today would therefore have created a price an operator can set and the
storefront cannot honour** — the same unit sold at one figure to a guest and displayed at another to staff.
That is a money contradiction, and a worse outcome than the missing feature. So the surface is deliberately
**not built**, and `NightlyRate` is deliberately **not wired into the charging path**.

⛔ **THE FOUNDER QUESTION THAT MUST BE ANSWERED BEFORE PHASE 2 — it is not "which UI", it is *when is the unit
chosen?*:**
1. **The guest picks the unit at booking** (units become individually sellable) — the honest way to charge
   per-unit, and a booking-flow change.
2. **The operator pre-assigns the unit** — per-unit pricing applies only to operator-created bookings; the
   storefront keeps type pricing, and the two must be visibly different things, not silently.
3. **Per-unit is planning-only** — it informs rack/owner views and never charges.

**Four mutations, each verified to land** (money makes this mandatory): preferring the type rate over a set
override reds the override tests; dropping the unit predicate so an override leaks to a sibling reds the
isolation test; resolving "no override" as €0 reds four tests including zero-movement; removing `unit_id`
from the unique key reds the duplicate test. ⚠️ The leak mutation **silently failed to apply on the first
attempt** — the pattern did not match, so its "pass" meant nothing. Re-applied and re-verified; §N.4p again.

**SEQUENCED, NOT BUILT (each its own pass):** the booking-flow decision above · wiring `NightlyRate` into the
charge path once that is settled · per-unit across the rates grid, calendars and reports · the D18-6 grid
re-shape the founder can now revisit · channel-sync (per-unit rates are **not** pushed to OTAs) · bulk
tooling. ⚠️ **The rack's "N units affected" safeguard is untouched and still accurate today** — with no
overrides, a type-level edit still affects every unit of the type; the moment overrides exist it must read
"units without their own price", and that is part of the phase-2 surface, raised here rather than changed
silently.

Suite **2357 / 2347**, 15,197 assertions, the same 9 non-green; PHPStan L5 (0); Pint clean.

## 2026-08-17 — D18-5 phase 2 · the override is CHARGED where the unit is committed before the money

⚠️ **FOUNDER RULING recorded: option 1 — guests book a specific unit.** That settles the product. It does not,
by itself, settle the code, and confirming the code first changed what this pass could honestly ship.

⚠️ **THE GUEST FLOW STILL DOES NOT CARRY A UNIT — CONFIRMED, NOT ASSUMED.** `BookingEngineController` validates
`room_type_id` + `rate_plan_id` and nothing else; `booking_quotes` has no unit column; `priceOver()` takes a
rate-plan id. So on the storefront the money is still decided before any unit exists, exactly as phase 1
found. **Wiring per-unit pricing there today would have re-created phase 1's contradiction**, so the guest
path is untouched and prices type-level, byte-for-byte as before.

⚠️ **BUT ONE PATH ALREADY SATISFIES THE RULING, AND THAT IS WHERE THIS SHIPPED.** The operator's New
Reservation controller takes a `unit_id` **and validates it against the offer before charging** — so the
guest's actual room is known at the moment money is decided. Per-unit pricing is therefore honest there
today, with no contradiction: the unit is chosen, the override is resolved for it, and the folio is charged
that figure.

**`NightlyRate::stayTotalForUnit()`** is the seam, and its **NULL return is the zero-movement guarantee**.
⚠️ It deliberately does not re-derive a stay total when no override exists, because rate plans can be
**derived** (`derived_from_rate_plan_id` + `adjustment`) — so the price a caller already computed is not
always the raw sum of `rate_calendar`, and recomputing it would have moved money nobody asked to change. No
override anywhere in the stay ⇒ NULL ⇒ the existing figure stands untouched. A partial override prices the
overridden nights at the unit price and the rest at the type price; **an unpriced night returns NULL rather
than being summed as zero**, so a stay is never quietly given away.

⚠️ **THE MUTATION THAT EXPOSED A HOLE IN MY OWN GUARDS.** Deleting the wiring from the charge path left every
test green — they proved the *resolver* answers correctly and said nothing about whether the money path asks
it. On a pricing change that is the only question that finally matters. A test now books through the real
operator route and reads the **folio**: the overridden unit is charged **€245.00**, its sibling **€180.00**.
Re-run, the deletion reds it.

⚠️ **AND TWO FIXTURE TRAPS, BOTH OF WHICH LOOKED LIKE PRODUCT BUGS.** The first booking silently created
nothing because `seedScenario` publishes availability only for **2026-09-01 → 2026-09-10** and the fixture sat
outside it. The second made the sibling appear to be charged the override — both bookings land in the same
second, so "the newest reservation" re-read the first one; the reservation is now identified by the unit it
occupies. Neither was the code.

**Eight mutations across both phases, each verified to land** (money makes that mandatory): prefer-type-over-
override · leak-to-sibling · no-override-as-€0 · inert unique key · return-a-total-when-there-is-no-override ·
sell-an-unpriced-night-free · **charge-path-ignores-the-override** · hasAny-ignores-the-unit.

⚠️ **ZERO EXISTING MONEY MOVED:** `rate_calendar` still hashes `2bbdafccc3b5c1ee43f89fe313a3f02d` (929 rows,
10,920,000 minor), the demo holds **zero** overrides, and §G.1, VAT and the computation were not touched.

⛔ **WHAT OPTION 1 STILL NEEDS, AND IT IS THE LARGER HALF — SEQUENCED, NOT BUILT:** the storefront must let a
guest *choose* a unit before checkout. That is not a UI job: it makes units individually sellable, which means
per-unit availability, a quote that carries `unit_id`, and — the dangerous part — `createBooking` reserving
**that exact unit** under lock without weakening the certified no-double-booking guarantee. Half-building it
would risk the one invariant this system protects most, so it is its own gate. ⚠️ **Channel-sync stays
sequenced too** — per-unit rates are not pushed to OTAs, and an OTA quoting a stale type price for an
overridden unit is the same contradiction in a place we cannot correct it. ⚠️ The "N units affected"
safeguard remains accurate while no overrides exist; it must read "units without their own price" as part of
that gate.

Suite **2362 / 2352**, 15,210 assertions, the same 9 non-green; PHPStan L5 (0); Pint clean.

## 2026-08-17 — D18-5 phase 3 · CONFIRM-FIRST DISSOLVED THE GATE: the guarantee is ALREADY unit-grain

⚠️ **FOUNDER RULING (option 1, guest-picks) re-recorded for phase 3.** This pass was framed as the dangerous
one — extend the certified no-double-booking guarantee to unit grain and prove it under concurrency, or stop.
**Reading the mechanism first showed there is nothing to extend: it is already there, and already proven.**

**How the guarantee actually works** (`AssignmentService`, read end-to-end rather than assumed):

- The mutex is `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` on the **`availability`** rows for `(room_type_id, each night)` — counts
  per room type (`total`/`sold`/`out_of_order`/`blocked`), which serializes every booking of that type.
- ⚠️ **`createBooking()` already accepts an optional `unit_id` per line**, and `occupy()` — the single locked
  core both `createBooking()` and `createGroupBooking()` funnel through — already guards it: it refuses a
  non-bookable unit **and calls `assertUnitFree()`**, a half-open overlap check on `reservation_units`
  (`check_in < out AND check_out > in`) taken **`lockForUpdate()` inside the same transaction**.
- So a specific unit is *already* protected at unit grain, by the same lock discipline, in the same
  transaction — not by a parallel or weaker check.

⚠️ **AND IT IS ALREADY CERTIFIED.** `tests/Feature/ConcurrentBookingTest.php` carries
*"permits exactly one of two truly-concurrent bookings on the same unit and dates"* — a real race, not an
assertion. Re-run during this pass: **1/1, 7 assertions, green.**

**So the hazard this gate was created for does not exist.** Nothing was changed, because changing the most
protected invariant in the system to add a guarantee it already provides would have been pure risk for no
gain. The correct output of a confirm-first pass is sometimes that the feared work is already done.

⚠️ **WHAT PHASE 3 ACTUALLY STILL NEEDS IS NARROWER, AND NOW LOW-RISK** — it is a plumbing job on the
storefront, not a concurrency job on the booking core:

1. `booking_quotes` gains a nullable `unit_id` (a type-only quote must keep resolving type-level).
2. The storefront offers the *specific available units* of the chosen type/dates and lets the guest pick one —
   availability shown must equal availability enforced.
3. That `unit_id` flows into `createBooking()`, **which already handles it safely** — this is the step that
   was feared and is in fact free.
4. `NightlyRate` is consulted for the chosen unit so the storefront charge is `charged = shown = resolved`,
   exactly as phase 2 did on the operator path.

⚠️ **NOT STARTED IN THIS PASS, DELIBERATELY.** That build spans a migration, the quote model, a storefront
selection UI and the charge seam, and its money claims need the same treatment phase 2 got — a real booking
whose **folio** is read, plus mutation proof that the charge path consults the resolver (phase 2's charge
wiring passed every test until a mutation exposed that nothing checked it). Beginning it at the end of a long
session and leaving it unverified would be exactly the half-built state phases 1 and 2 refused. It is its own
gate, and it is now a **safe** one.

**No code changed in this pass.** The finding is the deliverable: the blocker that made phase 3 dangerous
does not exist, and the remaining work can be planned as ordinary plumbing.

## 2026-08-17 — D18-5 · the rates-grid blast-radius label, reconciled for per-unit pricing

⚠️ **THE LEDGER CALLED IT "N units affected"; THE CODE NEVER SAID THAT.** Searching for that phrase found it
only in my own phase 1/2 entries. The safeguard is real but reads **"3 units"** on each room-type row of the
rates grid (`RatesGrid::row()` → `units_label`, fed by `withCount('units')`), and the grid's own docblock says
why it exists: *"so the operator is never misled about what a save touches."* Confirming the wording before
"fixing" it mattered — a text-matching fix would have found nothing and reported success.

**Why it needed reconciling.** A rate plan prices a ROOM TYPE, so one save moves every unit beneath it — the
count was exactly right while type-level was the only pricing there was. It became a small lie the moment a
unit could carry its own price (phases 1–2), because a type-level save does not reach an overridden unit.

**The fix:** the row now subtracts units carrying an override **for that plan, inside the displayed
fortnight** — the scope of the save being warned about. The source of truth is `unit_rate_overrides`, so this
cannot drift from what `NightlyRate` actually resolves (§N.8f). ⚠️ The unique-ing is done with `pluck` +
`unique` in PHP rather than `->distinct()->count()`, which has already returned 0 for every period once in
this codebase while looking exactly like a working guard (§N.27.7).

⚠️ **TRANSITION-CORRECT BY CONSTRUCTION, WHICH WAS THE ACTUAL DIFFICULTY.** With no overrides the subtraction
is zero and the label is **byte-identical to what it has always shown** — `"2 units"`, asserted to the
character, because a "fix" that reworded a warning already telling the truth would itself be a regression.
Only when something is genuinely excluded does it change shape: `"1 of 2 units · 1 priced individually"`.

⚠️ **AND THE WORDING FOLLOWS THE NUMBER.** Showing a reduced count under the old phrasing would be the same
misleading warning in a quieter form — the operator would read "2 units" and not know a third was untouched.
A mutation that does exactly that reds the tests.

**Three mutations, each verified to land:** counting all units regardless of overrides (the pre-fix
behaviour) reds the exclusion tests; dropping the date-window predicate reds the scope test — an override
three months out must **not** shrink today's warning; showing the corrected number under the old wording reds
both.

**Untouched:** the save behaviour, the rate write, `NightlyRate`, §G.1, isolation/RBAC. The demo carries zero
overrides, so its label is unchanged. Count and label only.

Suite **2366 / 2356**, 15,219 assertions, the same 9 non-green; PHPStan L5 (0); Pint clean.

## 2026-08-17 — D18-5 · per-unit rates surfaced where a rate is shown FOR A UNIT

Phase 2 made the charge honour a unit's own price. A surface still displaying the room-type figure for that
same unit would contradict what is actually charged — on the very page that names the unit. This closes that
on the display side.

⚠️ **THE INVENTORY MATTERED MORE THAN THE EDIT, AND TWO OF MY OWN GUESSES WERE WRONG.** Grepping every reader
of `rate_calendar` found eight, and the question is not "does it show a rate" but **"does it have a UNIT in
scope"**:

| surface | scope | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| `OwnerUnitDetail` | one specific `$unit` | ⚠️ **routed through the resolver** |
| `RevenueOnHold::forUnits($unitIds, …)` | takes **unit ids** | ⚠️ **routed through the resolver** |
| `OwnerMyUnits` | iterates `editableRoomTypes()` | type-scoped — **I guessed "per-unit" and was wrong** |
| `OwnerRates::card(RoomType $rt, …)` | room type | type-scoped, correct as-is |
| `RatesGrid` · `OperatorDashboard` · `StorefrontLanding` | room type / plan | type-scoped, correct as-is |

**Routing a type-scoped surface through a unit resolver would be wrong, not thorough** — the type price *is*
the right answer where no unit is named. Only the two genuinely unit-contextual surfaces changed.

**`RevenueOnHold` was the substantive one.** It is handed the ids of blocked (out-of-order) units and asks
"what revenue is this withholding" — so it summed the room-type price once per unit. With overrides live that
under- or over-states a unit priced individually. It now resolves per unit, falling back to the type price, so
a unit nobody priced individually contributes exactly what it always did.

⚠️ **A "MONEY LEAK" THAT WAS A FIXTURE GAP.** The first run returned **0** for every unit. Checked before
concluding: `seedScenario` never sets `default_rate_plan_id`, which `RevenueOnHold` reads — **the original
code returned 0 there too**. Not a regression; the fixture now sets it, and that is recorded in the test so
the next reader is not misled by the same zero.

⚠️ **A MUTATION THAT DID NOT RED, EXPLAINED RATHER THAN PAPERED OVER.** Removing the `?? type price` fallback
left the tests green — because `NightlyRate::forUnit()` **already falls back internally**, so it cannot return
null while a type price exists. The trailing `??` is belt-and-braces, and the invariant it guards is tested
one layer down (`UnitRateOverrideTest` — *"never treats a missing price as zero"*). Bypassing the resolver
entirely **does** red, which is the mutation that matters here.

**Zero movement:** the demo carries no overrides, so every one of these surfaces displays exactly what it
displayed yesterday. §G.1, VAT presentation, the computation and the resolver's own logic are untouched, and
the grid was **not** re-shaped (that remains its own item).

## 2026-08-17 — D18-6 / STRUCT-1 · the re-shape was not deferred; it was DECIDED. Not re-shaped.

⚠️ **THE BRIEF'S PREMISE — "the shape change was deferred as STRUCT-1 pending per-unit, now unblocked" — is
not what the record says, and the brief itself warned that this area's descriptions have been wrong twice.**
They were wrong a third time.

**What STRUCT-1 actually was** (`docs/WAVE4-INVENTORY.md:96`, verbatim):

> **STRUCT-1 grid decision** (decision, then S) — per-room-type rows (with "N units" sub-label) vs a
> 1-unit-per-room-type rule.

It was a **fork between two shapes**, to be decided before the grid was built — not a re-shape parked until
per-unit pricing existed. And it **was decided**, in favour of per-room-type rows; `RatesGrid`'s own docblock
records the decision and its reasoning: *"the design's per-physical-unit grid cannot be backed without
silently editing every unit under a room type. Each row here is a ROOM TYPE… The sub-label states how many
physical units sit under it, so the operator is never misled about what a save touches."* That sub-label is
the one reconciled two passes ago.

⚠️ **AND PER-UNIT PRICING DOES NOT AUTOMATICALLY UNBLOCK THE OTHER SHAPE — IT CHANGES WHAT AN EDIT MEANS.**
The original objection was that a per-unit grid would silently edit every unit under a type. Overrides remove
that specific objection and introduce a larger one: **on a per-unit grid, every rate edit would mint an
override.** A row is a unit, so saving a price for it can only mean "this unit's own price". Within a few
edits every unit is permanently detached from its type's pricing, the type rate stops being the thing that
moves prices, and the blast-radius warning reads "0 of 3 units" everywhere — the safeguard rendered useless
by the shape rather than by a bug.

⚠️ **That is a product decision, and it is NOT the one the founder made.** The ruling was *"two units of the
same room type MAY be priced apart"* — permission for the exception. A per-unit grid makes the exception the
default, which is a different claim entirely, and phases 1–3 have repeatedly shown that the distance between
those two is where the money goes wrong.

**So nothing was re-shaped.** No code changed; `rate_calendar` still hashes `2bbdafccc3b5c1ee43f89fe313a3f02d`
(929 rows, 10,920,000 minor). The grid keeps per-room-type rows, which is the decided shape and remains
correct: it prices the type, warns how many units that reaches, and — since two passes ago — excludes the
units that carry their own price.

⛔ **THE QUESTION FOR THE FOUNDER, if a per-unit grid is still wanted:** *should editing a rate on a unit row
create a per-unit override for that unit?* If **yes**, the grid can become per-unit rows and every edit mints
an override (say so in the UI, because it is irreversible in effect — that unit stops following its type). If
**no**, per-room-type rows are already the right shape and D18-6 is closed as-is. A third option — unit rows
that are read-only until explicitly "priced individually" — keeps both behaviours honest and is probably what
the design intends, but it is a design decision, not an inference I should make.

**Untouched:** every rate value, the resolver, the grid, §G.1, isolation/RBAC. Suite unaffected (no code
changed).

## 2026-08-17 — D18-6 / STRUCT-1 · a correction to my own entry above, and why the answer is still "not yet"

⚠️ **I CHECKED ONE AUTHORITY LESS THAN I SHOULD HAVE, AND IT PARTLY VINDICATES THE BRIEF.** The entry above
concluded from `WAVE4-INVENTORY.md` and the grid's docblock that STRUCT-1 was a decided fork, not a deferral.
That is true, but I did not consult `design/DIVERGENCE-REGISTER.md`, which is the authority on design gaps —
and it records the per-unit grid as a real divergence on `/app/rates` (an exact-match rebuild, task #100) with
the stated reason: *"per-unit grid needs per-unit rate data the model doesn't hold; the toolbar 'All units'
filter + 'Bulk edit' modal likewise…"*.

⚠️ **THAT STATED REASON IS NOW STALE.** D18-5 phase 1 gave the model exactly that data. So the brief's premise
— "the blocker is removed" — is right about the register's *recorded* blocker, and my entry above was too
absolute in saying the re-shape was never deferred. It was deferred here, for a reason that has since been
answered.

⚠️ **AND YET THE ANSWER IS STILL "NOT YET", FOR A DIFFERENT AND LARGER REASON.** The register's blocker was
about **data availability**. The remaining blocker is **semantics**: on a grid whose rows are units, saving a
price can only mean "this unit's own price", so **every edit mints an override** and permanently detaches
that unit from its type. Within a few edits the type rate stops being the thing that moves prices and the
blast-radius warning reads "0 of N units" everywhere. Per-unit data makes the grid *possible*; it does not
decide whether every edit should *create* an exception. The founder ruled that units **may** be priced apart —
permission for the exception, not a mandate to make it the default.

**Still nothing re-shaped, nothing moved:** `rate_calendar` hashes `2bbdafccc3b5c1ee43f89fe313a3f02d`

data"* to *"the data now exists; the open question is what an edit on a unit row means"* — recorded here
rather than silently rewritten, since the register is a design authority and this is a product call.

⛔ **THE DECISION, unchanged from the entry above but now correctly sourced:** on a unit-row grid, does
editing a rate create a per-unit override? **Yes** → per-unit rows are buildable now, and the UI must say each
edit detaches that unit. **No** → per-room-type rows stay, and this divergence is ratified rather than open.
**Third option** — unit rows read-only until a unit is explicitly "priced individually" — preserves both
behaviours and is most likely what the design intends.
